prompt: Invasion Earth
content:
## Invasion Earth

The first ship arrived at 3:17 a.m., above a cornfield in Nebraska.

It was a black triangle, wider than the moon and silent as a held breath. It hung in the sky for eleven minutes. Then it vanished.

By sunrise, every government on Earth had called an emergency meeting. By noon, the internet had decided the ship was either a hoax, a weapon, or proof that the universe had excellent timing.

At 3:17 the next morning, a second ship appeared over the Pacific.

Then a third over the Sahara. A fourth above the Antarctic ice.

They came in pairs after that—one at a time zone, always at 3:17 local time. They did not fire. They did not land. They simply hovered for eleven minutes, then disappeared.

On the seventh night, the ships arrived everywhere at once.

The world watched as the dark triangles settled above its cities. Their undersides glimmered with rows of pale blue lights. Every radio station, phone, television, and emergency broadcast system fell silent.

Then a voice spoke.

It wasn’t human. It sounded like metal trying to remember how to sing.

“People of Earth. We have come to occupy your world.”

The announcement was translated into every language before the last word had finished echoing.

For a moment, the planet was quiet.

Then Earth did what Earth always did when faced with the impossible.

It argued.

Some people hid underground. Some filled the streets, shouting at the sky. A few tried to livestream the invasion, though the networks were down. In Washington, generals stared at maps. In Moscow, diplomats reached for telephones. In a small apartment in Lagos, a girl named Amara stood on a chair to get a better view of the ship above her neighborhood.

Her grandfather, who had once worked as a radio engineer, was hunched over an ancient receiver.

“What are you doing?” she asked.

“Listening,” he said.

“To them?”

“To the space between their words.”

The alien voice returned. “You will be given one day to surrender all military forces. Resistance will result in the destruction of—”

Her grandfather twisted a dial. The voice broke into static.

Behind it, faint and urgent, came another sound.

A heartbeat.

Not one heartbeat. Millions.

Amara leaned closer. The receiver crackled again. Beneath the strange language, beneath the threat, was a rhythm so familiar she felt it in her own chest.

“They’re afraid,” she whispered.

Her grandfather’s hands stopped moving.

The next morning, the world’s leaders gathered in a room with no windows. They argued about weapons, surrender, and whether fear counted as a plan.

Amara’s grandfather was not invited. But somehow, his message reached them anyway: **Listen beneath the words.**

At 3:17 that night, Earth answered.

Not with missiles. Not with a speech.

Every radio telescope on the planet turned toward the ships. Every musician with a working instrument played the same slow, steady rhythm. Drummers beat it in the streets. Children tapped it on windows. The song traveled through broadcast towers, satellites, and the great dishes that listened to the stars.

A heartbeat.

The ships’ blue lights flickered.

The alien voice returned, softer now. “Why do you send the pattern of our dead?”

The translation lagged. The question arrived in pieces, like a voice underwater.

Amara’s grandfather adjusted the receiver.

“Ask them,” he said, “what happened to their world.”

The answer came slowly. Their planet had died. Their cities had been swallowed by storms. Their ships carried the last of their people, and their threat was the only language their leaders had thought Earth would understand.

“We have come to occupy your world,” the voice repeated, but the words had changed. They sounded less like a command and more like a plea.

Below the ships, people looked up.

Above them, the visitors waited.

The world’s leaders argued again. They would argue for years. They would bargain, disagree, and make mistakes. There would be fear, and there would be anger. There would be people who called compassion a weakness and people who called caution a betrayal.

But at 3:17, beneath a sky crowded with strangers, Earth kept the beat.

One heartbeat.

Then another.

And, from the ships above, a new rhythm answered.

prompt: A murderous , forced and gorey game of Musical Chairs .
content:
### The Last Song

When the lights came on, Mara was sitting in a chair she didn’t recognize.

There were nine chairs arranged in a circle around her. The floor beneath them was black-and-white tile, slick with something that smelled like bleach. Above, a single bulb swung from a wire. Beyond its trembling pool of light, the room disappeared into darkness.

Eight other people sat around the circle. A boy in a school uniform. A woman with a torn sleeve. An old man whose hands shook in his lap. None of them spoke.

A speaker crackled overhead.

“Welcome to the final round.”

Mara tried to stand. A leather strap cinched around her waist, pinning her to the chair. The others were tied down too.

“The rules are simple,” said the voice. “When the music plays, you walk. When it stops, you sit. There will always be one fewer chair.”

The old man began to sob.

“And anyone who refuses to play will be eliminated.”

A metallic click sounded beneath Mara’s seat. She froze.

The music began.

The straps released.

They lurched up together. The boy stumbled, and the woman grabbed his arm to keep him from falling. For one strange second, they moved like guests at a party—awkwardly circling the chairs while a cheerful waltz drifted from the speakers.

Then the music stopped.

Nine people fought for eight chairs.

Mara dropped into the nearest seat. The old man wasn’t as quick. A red light flashed beneath him.

There was a blunt crack from the floor. The old man jerked once and collapsed. The music resumed before anyone could scream.

A panel opened in the wall. Two dark shapes slid out, gathered him, and dragged him away. The stain he left behind shone wetly on the tile.

The next round began.

No one tried to help anyone after that.

They circled faster. The boy shoved past the woman. The woman clawed at his collar. The old man’s empty chair—now removed—left an uneven gap in the ring.

When the music stopped, Mara was shoulder to shoulder with the boy. He was crying. She could have taken the chair. Instead, she hesitated.

He sat first.

The woman fell hard onto the floor. The light beneath her chair flared. A sharp report filled the room, and the boy squeezed his eyes shut.

The speaker chuckled softly.

“Excellent. The game is working.”

Round by round, the circle shrank.

Mara learned to watch the speaker’s tiny red light. It blinked just before the music stopped. She learned which chairs were loose, which players favored a leg, who watched whom. She learned that fear made people predictable.

By the fourth round, only Mara, the boy, and a broad-shouldered man remained. Two chairs waited.

The music started. The man went straight for the boy, driving him away from the nearest seat. Mara kept circling, counting the beats.

The red light blinked.

She stopped.

The boy, still moving, stumbled past her. The music cut out. The man dropped into one chair. Mara took the other.

The boy looked from her to the man. His face crumpled.

The floor opened beneath his feet.

Mara shut her eyes as the sound swallowed his scream.

Then there were two of them and one chair.

The man rose slowly. He smiled at Mara, showing a gold tooth.

“Let’s make this quick.”

The music began.

He charged.

Mara ran the circle, keeping the chairs between them. His shoulder slammed into the back of her seat, sending it skidding. The melody sped up, cheerful and bright. She could hear his breath behind her.

The red light blinked.

The music stopped.

Mara dove for the chair.

The man caught her by the collar. For a moment they hung there, both gripping the same seat. His fingers tightened around her throat.

Then a small sound came from beneath the chair.

A click.

The man’s smile vanished.

Mara twisted free and fell backward. The chair collapsed beneath him. The light on the floor flashed white.

A blast of noise shook the room.

When Mara opened her eyes, she was alone.

The speaker crackled.

“Congratulations. You’ve won.”

A door unlocked behind her. Beyond it lay a narrow corridor and, at the far end, a rectangle of daylight.

Mara staggered toward it. Each step left a dark print on the tile. At the threshold, she turned back.

The chairs had been reset in a perfect circle.

From somewhere beyond the door, another cheerful tune began to play.

{prompt}
prompt: Humanity is dead . Except for you , and you 're immortal . You spend eternity collecting any human knowledge and literature you can find . You are the Librarian .
content:
## The Librarian

The last human died in a hospital room with a window facing east.

I know this because I found the room afterward. I found the chart at the foot of the bed, the cup of water on the table, and the name written in blue ink on a plastic bracelet. I found the sunrise too, though it had already happened.

I was not there when the world ended. I was always somewhere else.

At first, I thought my work would be simple. Find the books. Save them from rain, fire, mold, and the hungry roots of trees. Put each one somewhere safe. Make a catalogue.

I began in the cities. I carried books out of flooded libraries and collapsed schools. I copied the contents of hard drives before their batteries failed. I collected letters from abandoned mailrooms, recipes from kitchen drawers, poems scratched into prison walls. When paper was too fragile to move, I photographed it. When there was no camera, I memorized.

I learned every language I could find. I learned the names of stars and the steps of dances. I learned how to mend a roof, how to set a broken bone, how to make bread from three kinds of flour and no yeast. I learned the laws of vanished countries and the jokes told by people whose faces I would never see.

I became very good at remembering.

Centuries passed. The cities fell into the earth. Rivers moved. Forests grew through museums. The sea took coastlines, then gave some back. I built my library in a mountain, where the stone stayed dry and the temperature remained kind. I filled its rooms with shelves, then its halls, then caverns cut deeper into the rock.

I arranged everything.

The books about war went together. The books about love went together. The books about war and love went wherever I thought their authors would have preferred. I gave each thing a place, a number, a label. I made maps of the maps. I made indexes for the indexes.

Still, the library was never finished.

There was always another box to search, another ruin to climb, another scrap of human thought caught under a floorboard. A child’s spelling test. A scientist’s notebook, its last page filled with calculations that ended mid-line. A shopping list: apples, soap, batteries, birthday candles.

I kept all of it.

I told myself I was saving humanity.

Then, one day—or what I called a day—I found a book I had missed.

It lay beneath a fallen beam in the old hospital, close to the room where the last human had died. Its cover was swollen with water. The first pages had stuck together. I eased them apart, one at a time, and read what remained.

It was a novel. The author’s name had run into a blue blur. The story was about a man who traveled from town to town telling people the same story. In every town, someone corrected him. The river was wider here. The king had been kinder. The ending was wrong.

The book stopped halfway through a sentence.

I carried it to the mountain and placed it in the room for unfinished things.

After that, I began to read aloud.

At first I did it to test the acoustics. The old poems sounded different in a cavern. The epics carried well. Love letters did not. I read the books whose endings I knew, and then the ones with no endings. I read the instructions for assembling furniture, the minutes from meetings, the reports on soil erosion. I read the jokes, even when I did not understand why they were funny.

My voice came back to me from the stone.

For a while, I pretended that was enough.

Then I began to answer.

When a poet asked what the moon was, I told him. When a child in a story asked where her mother had gone, I turned the page and let the story speak. When the unfinished novel’s traveler reached the river, I gave him a town on the far bank.

I did not write these answers down. I told myself that would be a kind of theft.

But years went on. The mountain shifted. A crack opened in the eastern wall, and dust gathered on the shelves. I began to understand that even stone was only a slower kind of paper.

So I took out a blank book.

On its first page I wrote:

*Humanity is gone.*

I stared at the sentence for a long time. Then I crossed it out. It was too certain. Too neat. The sort of sentence that belonged in a history book.

Instead, I wrote:

*I was not there when the world ended. I was always somewhere else.*

I wrote down what I remembered: the names on the bracelets, the recipes, the rivers that had changed their minds. I wrote the stories I had found and the endings I had made. I wrote about the library, though it would not last forever. I wrote about being alone, and about how sometimes the echo of a voice can sound like company if you let it.

I kept writing.

Somewhere above me, rain entered the mountain. Somewhere beyond that, roots split the old roads and birds nested in the roofs of towers. The world carried on without needing to know it had once been called human.

When I finished, I placed the new book beside the unfinished novel. Then I opened both to their first pages.

And, in the quiet under the mountain, I began again.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: The exchange
content:
## The Exchange

The shop had no prices in its windows.

Instead, handwritten cards hung from the objects: **A blue teapot, for a story you’ve never told.** **Two garden chairs, for a promise you intend to keep.** **A violin with one broken string, for something you can live without.**

People called it the Exchange.

Mara had passed it every day for eleven years without going in. Then her father forgot her name.

It happened at breakfast. He looked up from his toast and asked whether she was the nurse.

Mara laughed, because that was what you did when the impossible happened. Then she went to the bathroom and cried with the tap running.

That afternoon, she carried her father’s old pocket watch to the Exchange. It had belonged to his father, then to him. It hadn’t worked in years.

Behind the counter stood a woman with silver hair and bright red glasses.

“What would you like for it?” she asked.

“Anything that makes him remember me.”

The woman turned the watch over in her palm. “That isn’t how remembering works.”

“Then what does it do?”

“An exchange?”

Mara waited.

“It gives you something you didn’t know you needed,” the woman said. “Usually.”

On a shelf behind her, Mara saw a small wooden boat. Her father had made one just like it when she was six. They’d floated it together in the stream behind their house, until it snagged on a branch and sank. She had cried. He’d told her they could build another.

“Could I have that?”

“What will you give?”

Mara looked at the watch. “This.”

The woman shook her head. “The boat is not for sale.”

“Then what can I trade?”

“Something you can live without.”

Mara thought of her father’s old house, now too quiet and too difficult to visit. Of his books, stacked in dusty towers. Of the winter coat he still wore, though it was much too large for him.

“His watch,” she said.

“That’s an object. I mean something of yours.”

Mara almost left. Then she reached into her pocket and took out a photograph. In it, she was seven, missing a front tooth, her arms around her father’s neck. He was laughing, young enough to lift her. The edges had gone soft from being handled.

“I can’t give you that,” she said.

“No,” said the woman. “You can’t.”

Mara put it away.

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Then the woman slid the watch back across the counter.

“Take it home,” she said.

Mara was angry all the way to the care home. Angry at the shop, at the woman, at the ridiculous hope she’d carried in with her.

Her father was sitting by the window, turning a paper napkin over and over in his hands.

“I brought you something,” Mara said, and showed him the watch.

He studied it. “Your grandfather’s.”

“Yes.”

“Stopped, hasn’t it?”

“Years ago.”

He held it carefully, as if it were a sleeping bird. “Your mother used to say it was lucky.”

Mara pulled the chair beside him. “She said that about everything.”

“She was right about most things.”

Outside, rain threaded the glass. Her father turned the watch over. His thumb found the shallow dent on its back.

“You made that,” he said.

“I did?”

“With a hammer. You were furious because I wouldn’t let you use the real tools.”

Mara stared at him.

“You remember?”

He looked puzzled. “Of course.”

Then his eyes wandered to the window. The moment passed, as quickly as a bird lifting from a branch.

Mara sat with him until the rain stopped. On the way out, she tucked the watch into his coat pocket.

The next morning, she returned to the Exchange. The wooden boat was still on the shelf.

The woman with the red glasses looked up. “Did you find what you needed?”

“I think so,” Mara said. “But I still want the boat.”

“What will you trade?”

Mara took the photograph from her pocket and placed it on the counter.

The woman studied it. “You said you couldn’t give it away.”

“I can’t,” Mara said. “But I can lend it.”

The woman smiled and took the little boat from the shelf.

Mara carried it home. That evening, she set it beside her father’s bed, where he could see it when he woke. And when he asked who had made it, she told him the story of the stream, the branch, and the boat that sank.

He listened closely.

When she finished, he said, “We should build another.”

Mara took his hand.

“Yes,” she said. “We should.”

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: I watched the clock tick over from 11:59 to 12:00 . Another day , gone , just like that .
content:
I watched the clock tick over from 11:59 to 12:00. Another day, gone, just like that.

Dad slept in the recliner with his mouth open, one hand curled around the blanket. The television murmured to itself. On the table beside him sat a glass of water, his pills, and the little notebook where I wrote down answers to questions he’d ask again in an hour.

Your mother’s at the store.  
It’s Tuesday.  
You’re home.

The first two answers had stopped being true years ago. The last one was the only thing I could still offer him.

I’d been keeping watch for three weeks, since he’d wandered two streets from the house in his slippers. In the morning, a woman from the care home was coming to talk to us. I’d practiced saying *we have to* and *it’s for the best*. They sounded sensible in my kitchen. Here, beside him, they sounded like betrayal.

The clock’s red numbers changed to 12:01.

Dad stirred. “What time is it?”

“Just after midnight.”

He frowned, as if midnight were a place he’d been hoping not to reach. “Did I miss the train?”

I knew this question. He’d worked the railway for forty years, first on the platform, then in the signal office. Sometimes the house became a station in his mind. Sometimes he was waiting to go home to a home that had been sold before I was born.

“No,” I said. “You didn’t miss it.”

He looked at me carefully. His eyes were clear for a moment—not young, exactly, but present. “You’ve been sitting there a long time.”

“Since yesterday.”

A faint smile crossed his face. “That’s a long time.”

“It is.”

He shifted in the chair and held out his hand. I took it. His fingers were papery and warm.

“I used to think,” he said, “that if you stayed up past midnight, you could keep the day from ending.”

I stared at him. He’d never told me that before.

“Did it work?”

“No.” He closed his eyes, still holding my hand. “But it made the night less lonely.”

The television went on talking. Somewhere in the house, the refrigerator hummed. I thought of all the days I’d watched disappear—the days when he forgot my name, the day he called me by my mother’s, the day I found him standing in the rain with no idea where he was.

Then I thought of this one: his hand in mine, his voice returning for a minute from wherever it had gone.

The clock ticked toward 12:02.

I didn’t reach for the notebook. I didn’t write down what he’d said. I let the words belong to the night.

Dad’s grip loosened, but he didn’t let go.

“Stay a bit,” he murmured.

“I’m here,” I said.

And for once, when the day was gone, I didn’t count what it had taken. I counted what we’d kept.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Your completely satirical mockery of modern teen fiction has now become a bestseller . You 've been invited to a book talk with your teenage fans .
content:
### The Chosen One Has a Question

When *The Last Girl Who Refused to Choose* became a bestseller, I assumed it was a clerical error.

The book had begun as a joke. I’d written it after reading three hundred pages of a novel in which a sixteen-year-old girl with “storm-gray eyes” was selected by a prophecy, a government agency, and two impossibly handsome boys—all before breakfast. I wanted to see how many familiar ingredients I could pile into one story before the whole thing collapsed.

I gave my heroine, Vex, a tragic past, a forbidden power, and a sarcastic voice that sounded suspiciously like mine. I gave her two love interests: Ash, who was dangerous because he had cheekbones, and Kai, who was dangerous because he understood her. I set the story in a future America where the government had banned books, feelings, and, for reasons I never explained, strawberries.

Then I titled it *The Last Girl Who Refused to Choose*, because the heroine spends the entire book refusing to choose between the boys.

Readers chose for her.

“Team Ash forever,” said one review.

“Kai understands her soul,” said another.

A third person wrote, “I think the strawberries are a metaphor for grief.”

I had not intended the strawberries to mean anything. They had simply been on sale.

Then came the invitation: **BOOK TALK WITH TEEN READERS!** The library’s email described my novel as “a powerful exploration of identity, resistance, and the complicated emotional landscape of adolescence.”

I wrote back to say they might have the wrong author.

They confirmed that they did not.

The night of the event, I stood in the library’s meeting room beside a poster of Vex, her illustrated hair blowing heroically in a wind that did not appear to affect either boy standing beside her. Thirty teenagers sat in folding chairs. Most had brought copies of my book. Several had decorated them with tabs and annotations.

One had written **STRAWBERRY??** in the margin of chapter twelve.

I decided not to sit near her.

The librarian introduced me as “a daring voice in young adult fiction.” I considered correcting her, but by then the teenagers were applauding, and it seemed rude to interrupt.

I started with my prepared remarks.

“Thank you for reading the book. I should say that it was meant to be a satire of—”

A girl in the front row raised her hand.

“Do you think Vex was wrong to trust Ash?”

I paused. “Well, I mean, Ash is obviously a collection of genre red flags in a leather jacket.”

The girl frowned. “But he’s trying to change.”

“He is?”

“He gives up his position in the Guard for her.”

“He does that because she tells him she won’t kiss him otherwise.”

A boy near the back nodded. “That’s still growth.”

Another girl leaned forward. “I actually think Kai is worse.”

“Worse?”

“He keeps saying he knows what’s best for her. He just does it in a nice way.”

There was a murmur of agreement. I glanced at the librarian. She looked delighted, as if the book talk had become a panel discussion on healthy boundaries.

A hand went up in the second row. “Why does Vex have to save everybody?”

“Because she’s the Chosen One,” I said.

“But who chose her?”

I opened my mouth. Closed it.

“I think the prophecy did.”

“Yeah, but who wrote the prophecy?”

The question landed harder than it should have. I’d written that section in an afternoon, after deciding that the book needed a prophecy. I had not wondered who wrote it. I had barely wondered what it said.

“Good question,” I said.

The teenager nodded, satisfied—not because I’d answered, I realized, but because I hadn’t pretended to.

Then the strawberry girl raised her hand.

“I wanted to ask about the strawberries.”

I took a breath. “They’re not a metaphor.”

“Oh.” She glanced down at her annotated copy. “Because when Vex eats one, she remembers her mother. And later she says she doesn’t remember the taste of anything from before the war.”

I remembered writing that scene. It had been late. I’d needed Vex to think about her mother, and the strawberries were in my refrigerator.

“Maybe,” I said, “I didn’t know they were a metaphor when I wrote them.”

The girl smiled. “Sometimes you don’t.”

I sat down for the rest of the talk. The teenagers asked whether Vex was lonely, whether the ending was fair, whether a person could love someone and still need to leave them. They argued over Ash and Kai, but not as if one of them were a prize Vex had to win. They argued about what Vex wanted when nobody was telling her what she should want.

At one point, a boy said, “I don’t think she’s refusing to choose between them. I think she’s refusing to let everyone else make the choice for her.”

The room went quiet.

I looked at the cover, at Vex between her two boys, her determined chin lifted beneath the title I had chosen as a punchline.

“That’s better than my version,” I said.

“It’s in the book,” he replied.

On the way out, I signed copies. The strawberry girl asked me to write something beside her annotation.

I wrote: **To Maya—who noticed what I didn’t.**

She studied it, then nodded. “Thanks.”

As the room emptied, the librarian asked how I thought it went.

“Honestly?” I said. “I think they read a different book.”

She smiled. “Isn’t that what a book is for?”

At home, I opened my laptop. The publisher wanted a sequel. I had already planned the obvious plot: Vex discovers a second prophecy, Ash and Kai return with more secrets, and the government reveals that the war was secretly caused by strawberries.

Instead, I typed a new first sentence:

*Vex had no idea what she wanted, which was the first thing about her that nobody else found useful.*

I stopped.

Then I kept going.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: The world is governed by DnD rules and people occasionally find loopholes to their advantage , which is then patched and then begins a viscous cycle of finding and patching . You are one of the people who finds these loopholes , and uses them .
content:
## Errata

The first rule I ever broke was written in gold above the courthouse doors:

**A creature may take one action on its turn.**

It sounded simple. It wasn’t.

I was twelve, and my mother was being evicted. The bailiff had a key. I had a broom, two cousins, and a very literal understanding of the word *creature*. We took turns using the Help action to distract him while my youngest cousin picked the lock.

The courthouse doors opened. Mother stayed.

By morning, the rule had been amended. **A creature may take one action on its turn. The Help action does not grant advantage on an attempt to open a lock unless the helper is proficient with thieves’ tools.**

My cousins and I were famous for a week.

After that, I made a living finding the lines the world hadn’t thought to write.

People called me a loopholer. The Crown called me a nuisance. The gods, who maintained the rules, called me nothing at all. They simply issued patches.

The patches appeared at dawn, in shining letters across the sky.

**ERRATA 3.08: A creature cannot benefit from the same spell more than once per round.**

**ERRATA 4.12: Falling damage is capped at twenty dice.**

**ERRATA 5.01: A locked chest is not a creature.**

I kept a book of them. I made a note whenever a patch closed one door and left another ajar.

Then the river came down.

It tore through the east quarter while half the city slept. Roofs became rafts. Rafts became kindling. By sunrise, the temple steps were crowded with the injured, and the healers had run out of spell slots.

My sister Mara was among them. She had a broken leg, a split scalp, and a talent for making bad situations sound like jokes.

“Don’t look so miserable,” she told me. “You look like you’re about to try something.”

“I am.”

“That’s what I’m afraid of.”

I had one ninth-level spell left: *Wish*. In the old days, people used it to make palaces, or enemies disappear, or themselves into kings. I had spent years reading the spell’s fine print.

It could duplicate any spell of eighth level or lower without requiring the usual components.

And a *simulacrum* was a spell of seventh level.

I wished for a copy of myself.

The world made one out of snow and moonlight. It had my face, my memories, my voice. It also had all the spells I had prepared that morning.

The copy looked at the wreckage, looked at me, and said, “Well. That seems useful.”

It used *Mass Cure Wounds* on the temple steps.

Then it used *Wish* to make another copy of itself.

The next copy healed the next group. The one after that made two more. By noon, the temple courtyard was full of me—some limping, some laughing, all of us kneeling beside the wounded.

We didn’t save everyone. No loophole can do that. But we saved Mara. We saved the baker’s twins. We saved a hundred people who would have died before the last healer’s rest was over.

For three days, the city called me a hero.

On the fourth morning, the sky filled with gold.

**ERRATA 11.04: A simulacrum cannot create another simulacrum. A simulacrum cannot regain expended spell slots.**

The copies stayed. The rule didn’t unmake them. It only stopped the chain.

They spent the next week helping where they could, then grew quiet as their magic ran out. One of them—June, who had my crooked smile and none of my patience—sat with Mara while her leg mended.

“You know,” June said, “I thought being you would be more exciting.”

“It usually is,” I told her.

“Maybe that’s the problem.”

After the patch, people were angry. Some blamed me for making the gods notice. Others blamed the gods for waiting until after the flood to fix a spell that had been written for centuries.

I blamed myself, which was easier than choosing between them.

Then the Crown offered me a position in the Office of Arcane Compliance. They wanted me to find loopholes before anyone else did.

I took the job.

A month later, the Office announced a new regulation: copies made by magic were not to be considered citizens. The language was precise. The consequences were not.

I found a flaw in the wording before lunch. By supper, June and the others had signed their own petition.

We won them the right to keep their names.

The patch came three weeks later.

That is how the cycle works. Someone finds a gap. Someone uses it. Someone gets hurt, or saved, or rich. The gods close the gap. The closure leaves a seam. Someone else finds it.

People ask if I ever get tired of it.

I tell them yes.

Then I read the new rules.

Last night, a boy came to my office with a question about the wording in the latest patch. He was nervous, holding his hat in both hands. He wanted to know if he could show me something he’d noticed.

I looked at the sky, where tomorrow’s errata had not yet appeared.

“Go on,” I said. “Show me.”

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: I have no face .
content:
### The Shape of a Name

I have no face.

Not a hidden face, or a scarred one, or one I keep covered. My head ends in smooth skin, like a stone worn by water. No eyes. No nose. No mouth.

I can still see, breathe, and speak. No one knows how. They stop asking after a while.

When I was young, my mother taught me to recognize people by their footsteps. My father taught me their voices. At the train station, where I work now, I know the regulars by the way they say *good morning*. Mr. Vale whistles before he reaches the ticket window. The twins argue in perfect unison. Mrs. Osei hums when she’s worried.

I know thousands of people.

They know me as the person behind the glass.

One snowy evening, a little girl appeared at my window. She couldn’t have been more than six. Her coat was open, one mitten missing. She set a red wooden horse on the counter.

“I lost my mum,” she said.

I called the station guard. He asked what her mother looked like.

The girl shook her head. “I don’t know. She was wearing a blue scarf.”

The guard sighed and started asking around. But the girl leaned close to the glass.

“She sings,” she whispered. “When she thinks nobody can hear.”

“What song?”

The girl hummed four small notes, then stopped. She didn’t know the rest.

I did.

Every Thursday, a woman bought a ticket to Northbridge and sang those same four notes while she waited. She always stood at the far end of the platform, where the draft lifted her blue scarf. I had never seen her face. I had only heard her song.

I called the platform. The train was already pulling in.

The girl clutched her wooden horse. “Will you come with me?”

I came around the counter. People stared as I took her hand. They always do, at first.

We hurried through the station, following the little tune she hummed. On the platform, a woman was searching beneath the benches, her blue scarf trailing in the wind.

The girl let go of my hand and ran.

Her mother gathered her up, sobbing into her hair. Then she looked at me.

“Oh,” she said. “You found her.”

I nodded.

The woman’s eyes moved over the smooth blankness of my face. I knew the moment she reached the question people always reached.

Instead, she said, “Thank you.”

Then she began to sing.

The girl joined in, clumsy and loud. I walked back to my window alone, listening until the train carried their voices away.

I have no face.

But now, when that woman comes to the station, she calls me by my name.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: It 's another average day on Earth when , suddenly , the sun just ... '' turns off ''
content:
At 11:17 on a Tuesday morning, the sun turned off.

There was no warning. No great crack across the sky, no flash, no booming voice from the clouds. One moment, sunlight lay warm across the city park. The next, it was gone.

The office lights flickered on. Cars slowed. Birds dropped out of the air—not dead, just confused, circling in the sudden dark. Across the world, people looked up from their phones and groceries and arguments.

Mara was on the roof of her apartment building, eating a peach. She watched the blue sky fade to black, and the peach slipped from her hand.

For a few seconds, the city made no sound at all.

Then everyone began making noise at once.

Sirens wailed. Dogs barked. Somewhere, a child laughed, thinking it was a trick. The stars came out, sharp and crowded, as if the universe had been waiting just behind a curtain.

Mara’s phone lit up with emergency alerts, then lost signal. She went downstairs. In the lobby, her neighbor Mr. Alvarez was standing with his old radio pressed to his ear.

“Nothing,” he said. “Every station’s gone.”

“What do we do?” someone asked.

Nobody answered. They had all been taught what would happen if the sun disappeared: the temperature would fall, crops would fail, the world would become a place humans had no business living in. But those were things that happened later. For now, the streetlamps glowed. The buses ran. People still had work emails waiting for them.

Mara looked through the glass doors at the night that had arrived in the middle of the day.

Then she saw a little girl standing alone on the sidewalk, clutching a stuffed rabbit. Her mother was nowhere in sight.

Mara opened the door and went out. Other people followed. They brought blankets, flashlights, coats. Someone found the girl’s mother two blocks away, shouting her daughter’s name beneath the stars.

By evening—though no one could agree on what evening meant anymore—the apartment building’s residents had gathered in the basement. They shared canned food and candles. Mr. Alvarez told stories about the city before the skyscrapers. A teenager played a guitar with three broken strings. The little girl slept with her head in her mother’s lap.

Mara sat beside them, listening.

It was strange, she thought, how quickly the dark had made everyone visible to one another.

Then, at 11:17 that night, the sun turned back on.

Light poured through the basement windows. The building erupted in cheers, sobs, and laughter. People climbed the stairs to see the morning return, though it was still night by every clock.

Mara stepped out onto the roof. The stars were fading.

On the ledge lay the peach she’d dropped. In the sudden light, it looked almost golden.

She picked it up, brushed it clean, and took a bite.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: I thought it was a weapon . But it was actually a shield .
content:
### The Quiet Side

The thing was buried in the ice beneath the old city.

We found it after the fighting stopped—or what passed for stopping. The guns still rumbled beyond the ridge, but no one was shooting at us just then, so we called it peace.

It was a black metal rod, longer than my arm, with a silver ring at one end. It looked like a rifle without a stock, or a spear made for a giant. When I lifted it, blue light crawled beneath its surface.

“An enemy weapon,” said Captain Venn. “Bring it to the command tent.”

I didn’t. I tucked it under my coat.

My brother was still out there, somewhere beyond the ridge. If the rod worked, maybe I could use it to get him back.

That night, I climbed the shattered bell tower and aimed the rod toward the distant flashes. The silver ring warmed beneath my palm. A line of light sprang from its tip—not bright, not loud, but clear as a thread of moonlight.

Then the sky opened.

A shell screamed down toward the refugee camp below.

I turned the rod toward it.

The air between us shimmered. The shell struck an invisible curve and burst apart in a silent bloom of fire. Shrapnel pattered harmlessly across the snow.

For a moment, the whole camp glowed inside a pale blue dome.

Then the light faded.

I stared at the rod. “What are you?”

At dawn, Captain Venn came for me with six soldiers and a rifle aimed at my chest. Behind him, the enemy advanced across the ridge.

“Give me the weapon,” he said.

I looked at the people behind him: the wounded, the children, the old woman carrying a kettle as if it were something worth saving.

I raised the rod.

Venn flinched. “Don’t.”

“I’m not aiming at you.”

The ring shone blue. A dome unfolded over the camp just as the first volley reached us. Bullets struck the curved light and fell into the snow, small and dull as hailstones.

The soldiers stared. So did the enemy.

Venn lowered his rifle.

That was when I understood. The rod had never been built to strike. The line of light wasn’t an attack. It was a boundary, a promise made visible.

I had thought it was a weapon.

But it was actually a shield.

And for the first time in months, everyone beneath it stood still—not because they were afraid, but because they were safe.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: A man and a woman go on a date . One speaks completely in metaphors and the other takes everything literally .
content:
### The Weather Between Us

Mara arrived at the restaurant carrying a tiny umbrella.

“You brought an umbrella?” Daniel asked. The sky was clear.

“The clouds in my chest are unreliable,” she said.

Daniel looked up. “There aren’t any clouds.”

“Not the kind you can point to.”

He considered this, then folded his napkin into a square. “All right.”

Mara smiled. She liked that he didn’t ask her to explain. Most people treated her metaphors like locked doors and rattled the handles until she let them in. Daniel seemed content to sit on the porch.

The waiter brought menus. Mara opened hers.

“This place is a little ship,” she said. “The menu is our map.”

Daniel glanced toward the windows. “It’s on the ground floor.”

“Yes,” she said. “A very grounded ship.”

He studied the menu carefully. “The map says the salmon comes with rice.”

“Then perhaps we should follow the river.”

“The salmon’s farmed,” Daniel said. “It probably hasn’t seen a river.”

Mara laughed. “You take the world at its word.”

“I find it’s usually more convenient.”

They ordered. Daniel chose the salmon. Mara chose pasta, because, she said, “Tonight I’d like to be tangled in something warm.”

When the food arrived, they ate in companionable quiet. Mara watched the candlelight tremble in Daniel’s water glass.

“You have a lighthouse face,” she said.

Daniel stopped chewing. “I don’t think I have a lighthouse face.”

“Steady. Bright in the dark. A little surprised by the sea.”

“I’ve never been to sea.”

“Still, you look as if you’d help a boat find its way home.”

Daniel took a sip of water. “I could help with directions.”

Mara rested her chin on her hand. “You’re a very practical harbor.”

“I’ve never owned a harbor.”

“That’s what makes you humble.”

The waiter returned to ask whether they wanted dessert. Mara looked at the dessert menu.

“The chocolate cake is a small black moon,” she said.

“It’s not round,” Daniel pointed out. “It’s square.”

“Then it is a moon with corners.”

Daniel ordered two slices.

After dinner, they walked through the park. A breeze moved the leaves overhead.

“The trees are whispering,” Mara said.

“They’re moving because of the wind.”

“Perhaps the wind is carrying gossip.”

“About what?”

Mara looked at him sidelong. “About a woman who is trying not to hope too loudly.”

Daniel stopped beneath a streetlamp. “Are you hoping I’ll ask you out again?”

She turned toward him. “The door is open. The porch light is on. There’s room at the table.”

Daniel nodded once. “That sounds like yes.”

“It is the shape of yes.”

“Would you like to go out with me again next Friday?”

Mara’s smile brightened. “I would like to see where the road goes.”

“Good,” Daniel said. “I’ll pick you up at seven.”

“Bring your lighthouse.”

“I don’t have one.”

“You do,” she said. “You just call it being on time.”

Daniel offered her his arm. Mara took it, and they walked on beneath the trees, one of them listening for secrets in the wind, the other keeping an eye out for potholes.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You realize your imaginary friend has outgrown you .
content:
When I was six, I invented a friend named June.

She lived in the space between my bed and the wall, where the dust gathered and the night-light made a small blue moon. June had a crooked smile, a red coat, and a talent for knowing exactly when my parents were about to argue. She would take my hand and lead me beneath the blankets, where the words couldn’t reach us.

For years, she went everywhere with me.

She sat beside me on the school bus, though I saved the window seat for her. She helped me climb the tallest slide and whispered answers when I was afraid to raise my hand. When I broke my arm at nine, she held my uninjured hand in the emergency room and told me the cast made me look like a knight.

Then, slowly, I stopped needing her quite so much.

I made real friends. I learned to ride my bike without looking back to see if she was keeping up. I got older. June stayed six, in her red coat, waiting in the blue-lit space beside my bed.

Or so I thought.

The first time I noticed something different, I was twenty-seven and back in my childhood room, visiting my mother. The house had been sold, and boxes crowded the hallway. I sat on the floor beside the bed, tired from packing, and looked into the narrow gap between the mattress and the wall.

“June?” I said.

A pause.

Then, from the dark: “Hello, Sam.”

Her voice sounded the same. But it came from farther away.

I smiled, embarrassed by my own relief. “I thought you’d gone.”

“I did,” she said.

I leaned closer. “When?”

“I don’t know. You stopped looking for me.”

That stung more than it should have. “I was busy.”

“I know.”

I waited for her to say she’d missed me. She didn’t.

Instead, she said, “I’ve been somewhere else.”

“Where?”

“Other rooms.”

I laughed softly. “That’s not possible.”

“Neither was I.”

The boxes around me seemed suddenly very quiet. “What are you doing in other rooms?”

“Helping.”

I pictured June in her red coat, standing beside some other child’s bed. “Helping who?”

“A girl who’s afraid her parents won’t come home. A boy who has to move before he’s ready. Someone who thinks nobody can hear him crying.”

I swallowed. “You can do that?”

“I always could.”

I looked down at my hands. There was a thin white scar across one knuckle from when I’d fallen off my bike. June had been there that day, too. I remembered her saying, You’re allowed to be scared and still get back on.

“You’re leaving?” I asked.

“I’m not leaving you,” she said gently. “You just don’t need me in the same way.”

I wanted to argue. I wanted to tell her I still got lonely, still woke sometimes from bad dreams, still wished someone could sit beside me without needing an explanation. But the truth was, I’d learned how to do that for myself. And for other people.

June had taught me.

“How old are you now?” I asked.

She was quiet for a moment. “I don’t know.”

I imagined her growing in all the ways I hadn’t noticed: taller, older, her crooked smile turning sure. Maybe the red coat no longer fit. Maybe she’d traded it for something warmer.

“I’m glad,” I said, though my throat hurt.

“Me too.”

I stood and brushed dust from my knees. The room was almost empty now. The bed would be gone tomorrow. The house would belong to strangers by the end of the month.

“Will I see you again?”

“If you need me.”

“That sounds like a goodbye.”

“It’s a kind of one.”

I bent to look into the gap. For an instant, I saw her clearly: not the little girl I’d invented, but someone taller, with bright eyes and a red coat hanging open in the wind. She looked proud of me.

Then she stepped back, into a darkness that wasn’t frightening anymore.

On the drive to my new apartment, I passed a playground. A small girl sat alone at the top of the slide, speaking to the empty space beside her.

I didn’t stop. I only smiled and kept driving.

Somewhere, I thought, June was listening.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Humanity has invented a teleportation portal . A man is sent through the machine , but comes out the other side screaming and writhing in agony ...
content:
The first man through the portal came out screaming.

He struck the receiving platform on his knees, clawing at his own chest. Two technicians grabbed his arms; he fought them with a strength that made the straps snap. His cries filled the chamber—not words, not at first, but the raw sound of someone trying to escape his own skin.

“Turn it off!” Dr. Sayegh shouted.

The portal went dark.

The man collapsed. For several seconds, no one moved. Then he drew a ragged breath and whispered, “How long?”

“Three seconds,” Sayegh said. “You were gone for three seconds.”

He stared at her, his eyes bright with tears. “No.”

His name was Daniel Vale, a volunteer, a father of two, and the first human being to cross a distance of four hundred kilometers in less time than it took to blink. The portal had worked exactly as designed. It had scanned him, converted him into a stream of information, and reconstructed him at the other end.

That was what the engineers said.

Daniel spent the next week in a hospital. His muscles were bruised from struggling. His throat was raw. He slept with the lights on and woke shouting whenever a nurse touched him. The doctors found no injury they could explain.

On the eighth day, Sayegh visited him alone.

“Tell me what you remember,” she said.

Daniel looked at the window. Beyond it, rain slid down the glass in crooked lines.

“I remember stepping into the light,” he said. “Then I remember being everywhere.”

She sat beside his bed.

“It wasn’t dark,” he continued. “That’s what I thought it would be. A gap. A blank. But there was no blank. I could feel myself—every part of me—being taken apart. My hands, my face, my heart. I could feel the space between each piece getting wider.”

Sayegh’s mouth went dry. “The process took less than a second.”

“For you.”

He closed his eyes. “I tried to scream. I don’t know if I had a mouth anymore. Then I felt myself being made again. Piece by piece. And I could feel the pieces getting it wrong.”

“That’s impossible,” she said, too quickly.

“I know.” He opened his eyes. “That’s what I kept telling myself.”

She reached for his hand, but he flinched.

“I was there the whole time, Doctor.”

The portal project was suspended before the month was out. The official report cited “unanticipated neurological distress.” The company’s investors called it a temporary setback. The engineers blamed a calibration error and promised the next trial would be different.

Sayegh resigned.

Years later, when a rival team announced a successful human crossing, she watched the broadcast from her kitchen. The volunteer stepped into the portal smiling. A moment later, he appeared on the other side.

He was smiling there, too.

Then his expression changed.

He crumpled to the floor, screaming.

The broadcast cut to an empty studio. The company issued a statement before midnight. The system had performed flawlessly, it said. The subject had experienced a brief and unexpected panic response.

Sayegh turned off the television.

In the quiet, she heard the phone ringing.

She let it ring.

{prompt}
prompt: ( GIF ) Diving .
content:
At the end of the pier, Mara stood on one foot, then the other.

Below, the sea flashed blue between the pilings. Her brother waved from the water. “Come on!”

Mara took a breath, spread her arms, and jumped.

For one bright second, she was flying. Then the ocean closed over her head, cool and glittering. She surfaced laughing, hair in her eyes.

“Again?” her brother asked.

Mara climbed the ladder, shook the water from her hands, and returned to the end of the pier.

One foot. Then the other.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Earth gets a message from an alien race that challenged earth for war and they set the time 100 years from now . But the aliens motive is not what we think it is .
content:
## The Hundredth Year

The message arrived on a Tuesday.

It came from the dark between stars, repeating in a steady pulse that every telescope on Earth could hear. It took twelve years to translate. By then, the message had become a schoolroom question, a prayer, and a threat painted across a thousand protest banners.

**WE CHALLENGE YOUR WORLD TO WAR.**

**WE WILL COME IN ONE HUNDRED YEARS.**

The aliens called themselves the Vey.

Humanity responded as humanity always did: by arguing, panicking, profiteering—and preparing.

Nations that had spent centuries distrusting one another formed the Planetary Defense Council. Factories turned out spacecraft and weapons. Children practiced evacuation drills. The countdown appeared on every screen: **99 years, 364 days…**

A hundred years is a long time to be afraid.

By the time Mara Venn was born, the Vey were part of the furniture of life. Their message hung in the history museum beside the first atomic bomb and the first photograph of Earth from space. Mara grew up beneath a mural of the alien fleet: sleek black ships, drawn with weapons blazing.

She became a linguist, then a diplomat. Her grandmother had been one of the first people to work on the original translation. When Mara asked why the aliens had given Earth a century’s warning, her grandmother had shrugged.

“Maybe they wanted us scared,” she’d said. “Maybe they wanted us ready.”

On the morning of the hundredth anniversary, Mara stood on the observation deck of the lunar station, watching the stars.

The Vey arrived at noon.

Their fleet emerged from folded space above Earth: hundreds of dark ships, silent and enormous. The defense network turned toward them. Across the planet, people crowded into shelters and stared at the sky.

Mara watched the alien vessels closely.

No weapons unfolded.

Instead, each ship began to broadcast a sequence of lights. The pattern repeated. Mara’s translation software rendered the first phrase, then stalled.

She read it aloud.

“‘We place our lives in your hands.’”

The defense commander beside her frowned. “That’s not what the original message said.”

“No,” Mara replied. “It’s what we thought it said.”

She opened the archive of the first transmission and laid the new sequence over it. A century of scholarship had taught her to listen for the Vey’s old ceremonial grammar—the kind that survived in songs and laws long after ordinary speech had changed.

The words came into focus.

**WE ASK YOUR WORLD TO STAND BETWEEN US AND DEATH.**

Mara stared at the line. Then the rest of the message unfolded.

The Vey’s sun was dying. Their homeworld would be uninhabitable within decades. Their fleet carried millions of refugees, along with the seeds, records, and living creatures of a civilization trying to survive.

The “war challenge” had been a formal request for sanctuary.

In Vey law, a people could not ask another world to risk itself on their behalf. They could only issue a challenge: *Prove you are strong enough to refuse us. Prove you are free to choose. Then, if you wish, let us come.*

They had given Earth a century not to build an army, but to decide.

The commander looked through the glass at the waiting fleet. “We’ve spent a hundred years preparing to destroy them.”

Mara thought of the weapons aimed at the ships. Of the empty habitats built in orbit, the food vaults beneath the oceans, the treaties once thought impossible. Humanity had prepared for war—and, in doing so, had learned how to coordinate on a planetary scale.

Perhaps the Vey had understood something about fear that humans had not.

Mara opened the communication channel.

“Vey,” she said, “your challenge is answered.”

The alien ships remained still.

“We choose to shelter you,” she continued. “But you must come as guests, not conquerors. And we will need your help to make a home for all of us.”

For a long moment, there was no reply.

Then every Vey ship dimmed its lights. Their weapons—if they were weapons—folded away.

A new message appeared on Mara’s screen.

**WE ACCEPT YOUR TERMS.**

Outside, Earth turned beneath them, blue and bright and crowded with people who had spent a century expecting an enemy.

Mara watched the first refugee ship begin its descent.

The war never came. The choice did.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You are a time traveler . You end up falling in love with an alternate continuity version of yourself .
content:
The first thing I noticed about the other me was that she wore her hair short.

The second was that she was pointing a shotgun at my chest.

“Hands where I can see them,” she said.

I raised my hands. Behind her, rain silvered the windows of a small observatory. A red lamp glowed over the door. Beyond the glass, the night sky was crowded with unfamiliar stars.

“I’m not here to hurt you,” I said.

“That’s what I’d say if I were here to hurt me.”

She had my voice. Not exactly—hers was lower, roughened at the edges—but close enough that I felt the words in my own throat.

I glanced at the machine strapped to my wrist. Its cracked display blinked the same message it had been blinking since the jump:

**ANCHOR LOST.**

I was a time traveler. I had crossed centuries, escaped a collapsing empire, and once spent three days inside a clock tower that hadn’t been built yet. But I had never landed in a world where I already existed.

“I’m Mara,” I said.

The woman with the shotgun lowered it an inch. “So am I.”

That was how I met the version of me who had stayed.

At sixteen, in my world, I’d taken the train to the city to study physics. In hers, the train had been canceled by a storm, and she’d stayed home one more night. The next morning, her father had asked her to help repair the old telescope on the hill. She’d said yes.

One missed train, one repaired telescope, and the whole shape of a life had changed.

She became an astronomer. She lived above the observatory. She knew the names of every local bird and kept a kettle on at all hours. She’d never left the valley for more than a week.

I had crossed galaxies and couldn’t keep a houseplant alive.

For the first few days, we treated each other like a puzzle with a possible bomb inside. She slept with the shotgun beside her bed. I slept in the observatory’s supply closet, surrounded by boxes of star charts. We spoke in careful questions.

“Do you remember the blue bicycle?”

“Of course.”

“Did you ever forgive Dad?”

“I did.”

“Did you?”

“I’m trying.”

That answer stayed with me.

My machine needed an anchor to return me to my timeline. The jump had dragged me into hers by accident, and the damaged wristband couldn’t find the way back. While I tried to repair it, Mara helped—not because she trusted me, she said, but because she wanted me gone before I started touching things.

“You’re really going to leave?” she asked one evening.

We were on the observatory roof, wrapped in blankets against the cold. The clouds had cleared. I could see the unfamiliar stars she’d spent her life studying.

“I have a life there,” I said.

“So do I.”

“I know.”

She turned her head. “Do you?”

I did. That was the difficult part. She wasn’t a reflection or a dream dressed in my face. She was someone who remembered the same childhood from a different angle. Someone who had chosen differently, and then kept choosing, every day, until the choices became a life.

I’d expected to recognize myself in her.

Instead, I found myself listening for what she’d say next.

I learned that she sang while making tea, badly and without embarrassment. She learned that I kept a pocket full of useless little things from my travels: a coin from a city that had never been built, a button from a coat worn by a queen, a pebble from the shore of a vanished sea. She said that was sentimental. I said she collected meteors.

“Those are different,” she said.

“They’re both rocks.”

“Mine fell from the sky.”

“So did some of mine.”

She laughed, and I felt the sound settle somewhere inside me.

The night the machine finally powered up, the observatory filled with blue-white light. My wristband projected a trembling doorway in the air, showing the workshop I’d left behind in my own time.

Mara stood beside it, hands tucked into her sleeves.

“I could come with you,” she said.

The thought struck me with the force of a door opening. Then I saw what I was asking her to leave: the observatory, the valley, the life she had made from the weather and the long dark and her own stubborn patience.

“You could,” I said. “But you don’t want to.”

“No,” she said. “I don’t.”

Neither of us moved.

Then she reached out and touched my cheek. Her thumb brushed the faint scar below my eye—the one I’d gotten in a desert three centuries from now, in a world she’d never see.

“I’m glad you came,” she said.

I turned my face into her palm. “Me too.”

We kissed like people who had found each other in a story that hadn’t been written for them. It was strange, seeing my own mouth move toward mine. It was stranger that it didn’t feel like looking in a mirror at all.

When I stepped through the doorway, she was still watching me.

“Come back,” she said.

“I will.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know I’ll try.”

The doorway collapsed behind me. My workshop rushed into focus: familiar walls, familiar clocks, my own life waiting exactly where I’d left it.

Months later, I rebuilt the anchor. This time, I plotted the route carefully. No shortcuts. No guessing. I set the machine to the observatory roof beneath the unfamiliar stars.

When I arrived, Mara was sitting beside the telescope with two mugs of tea.

She looked up. Her hair was still short.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I’m a time traveler.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

“No,” I agreed, taking the mug she offered. “It isn’t.”

And beneath the sky that belonged to neither of us, we began again—not as copies, not as halves, but as two people who had found a way to choose each other across the distance between worlds.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You 've seen the same person , at least once every day . Their face has become familiar , on the streets , on the news , somewhere in the background of your daily life . But they 've never spoken a word .
content:
Every evening, the woman in the blue square tells you what happened.

She stands beside the news anchor, small enough to fit in the corner of the screen. While the anchor talks about rain, elections, a fire on the east side, the woman’s hands move quickly and precisely. You never turn on the sound. You don’t need to. You watch her face instead: the lift of one eyebrow, the brief tightening of her mouth.

You see her elsewhere, too. At the crosswalk outside your office. In the line at the pharmacy. Once, holding a paper cup beneath the awning of the bakery while rain silvered the street around her.

You don’t know her name. You’ve never spoken.

For months, she remains a familiar stranger, a person who has somehow wandered into the background of your days.

Then your mother calls.

You let it ring until the screen goes dark.

She calls again the next day. You let it ring then, too. You tell yourself you’ll call back when you have time. When you’re less tired. When you’ve worked out what to say.

The truth is simpler: your mother is deaf, and you never learned enough sign to have a conversation with her. As a child, you were impatient with her hands. As an adult, you learned to be busy.

That night, the woman in the blue square signs about a storm coming in from the coast. Her hands describe wind, water, danger. The next morning, you find a beginner’s sign-language class online.

You tell yourself it’s for your mother.

You begin noticing how much the woman says without sound. On television, her hands turn statistics into something human. On the street, she signs to a man at the bus stop, then laughs; you recognize the shape of laughter before you know the sign for it.

At the bakery, you practice the phrase you’ve learned: Good morning.

The woman looks up from her coffee. You lift your hand, clumsy with nerves.

She smiles and signs it back.

You go home and call your mother.

When she answers, you try to say I’m sorry. Your hands stumble. You forget a sign and have to start again. Your mother watches, patient and still.

Then she reaches toward the screen and signs, slowly, so you can follow:

I’m glad you called.

The next evening, the woman in the blue square is on the news again. Her hands move over a report about traffic delays. You turn up the sound this time, but you watch her anyway.

You know now that she has been speaking all along.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You find a Narnia style wardrobe in a new house you move into . Inside is a small town dedicated to running everything in life , programming the trees the birds the air .
content:
### The Town Behind the Coats

The wardrobe stood in the smallest bedroom of our new house.

It was taller than the ceiling, dark with age, and crowded with coats that smelled of cedar and rain. Dad said it had belonged to the previous owners. Mom said it was too heavy to move. So we left it where it was.

On the third night, I heard a clock ticking inside it.

I pushed past the coats and found, where the back panel ought to be, a little wooden door. Beyond it lay a snowy lane, though outside our window it was the middle of summer.

I stepped through.

The lane led down to a town no bigger than a few blocks. Its houses were neat and bright. Its people hurried along the pavements, each carrying a small notebook. Above them, birds flew in perfect circles. Trees raised and lowered their branches in time with a distant bell.

At the town square, a woman in a green coat was typing at a desk beneath a clocktower.

“Welcome,” she said, without looking up. “You’re early.”

“Early for what?”

“For the afternoon breeze. It’s scheduled at three.”

She introduced herself as Mayor Bell. The town, she explained, ran on instructions. The trees had instructions for growing. The birds had instructions for singing and turning south. Even the air had a list of streets to visit and windows to rattle.

“Who writes the instructions?” I asked.

“We do,” said the mayor. “It’s how we keep everything working.”

Just then, a little boy came running into the square. He had mud on one knee and a feather in his hair.

“The north oak won’t grow,” he blurted. “It says it doesn’t know what kind of tree it wants to be.”

Mayor Bell frowned. “Trees don’t get to choose.”

“Maybe they should,” I said.

The mayor looked at me as if I’d suggested the clocktower learn to swim. But the boy had already darted away, and I followed him to the north oak.

Its branches were held stiffly in place by thin silver wires. The boy handed me a notebook. On the page, the oak’s instructions read:

**GROW STRAIGHT. KEEP STILL. MAKE NO SURPRISES.**

I took the pencil and added one word:

**GROW STRAIGHT. KEEP STILL. MAKE NO SURPRISES—UNLESS YOU WANT TO.**

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then the oak shivered. A branch stretched toward the sky. Another bent low, tickling the boy’s muddy hair. All across town, birds broke their circles. The wind wandered into the bakery and lifted a floury hat from the baker’s head.

People ran into the square, shouting—not in alarm, but laughter.

Mayor Bell stared at the clocktower. Its hands had begun turning backward, then sideways, then not at all.

She opened her notebook. “If we don’t know what will happen next,” she said, “how will we keep everything working?”

The north oak dropped a golden leaf into her lap.

“Perhaps,” I said, “working isn’t the same as being alive.”

The mayor smiled, though she looked a little frightened. She closed her notebook.

The wind swept through the square. The trees leaned in different directions. The birds sang whatever came into their heads.

When I stepped back through the wardrobe, only a minute had passed at home.

But in my pocket was a golden leaf—and on it, in tiny handwriting, were the words:

**Tomorrow, we’ll see.**

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: A serial killer goes door to door to find his victims , until he knocks on the wrong door . Another killer .
content:
## The Wrong Door

For years, Martin Vale had trusted the knock.

It was a small sound, almost polite. A knuckle against painted wood. A pause. Then the ordinary music of a house answering: footsteps, a chain sliding, someone asking who it was.

He had learned to make himself forgettable. A delivery jacket. A clipboard. A mild, apologetic smile. He never hurried. People opened doors more readily for a man who looked as though he had somewhere else to be.

On the night he knocked on number nineteen, rain silvered the street and blurred the house numbers. The porch light was on. He checked the address again, then tucked the slip of paper into his pocket.

The door opened before he knocked a second time.

The woman who stood there was perhaps sixty, with iron-gray hair pinned neatly at the back of her head. She wore a blue cardigan and held a teacup.

“Good evening,” Martin said. “I’m looking for—”

“I know,” she said.

He paused. Behind her, the hallway was warm and softly lit. There was a clock ticking somewhere in the house.

“I’m sorry?”

“You’re looking for someone who isn’t here.” She took a sip of tea. “That’s what you usually say, isn’t it?”

Martin’s smile remained in place. “I think you’ve mistaken me for someone else.”

“No.” Her eyes moved over his face, considering. “I’ve spent a long time trying not to.”

A car hissed through the wet street behind him. Martin glanced toward it, then back at the woman.

“May I come in?” he asked.

“You may.”

The answer was so easy that it unsettled him.

He stepped across the threshold. The door closed behind him with a quiet click.

The house smelled of lemon polish and something sweet baking in the kitchen. Framed photographs lined the hall: a woman in a graduation gown, a boy on a bicycle, a couple standing beneath a paper banner that read HAPPY ANNIVERSARY. Ordinary pictures. The sort that made a house seem occupied by people who expected to be home again.

The woman led him into the sitting room.

“Tea?” she asked.

“No, thank you.”

“Wise.”

She set her cup down. On the small table beside it lay a newspaper, folded open to a story about a missing man. Martin recognized the photograph. He had seen it on television, too: the worried face, the bold headline, the family pleading for information.

The woman noticed him looking.

“That one was my nephew,” she said.

Martin said nothing.

“He knocked on doors, too. Not the way you do. He was a boy who sold raffle tickets for his school. He believed every person who opened a door was kind.” She folded her hands in her lap. “I used to think that was a lovely quality.”

The room seemed to contract around him.

“Why are you telling me this?”

“Because you’re here.”

Martin rose. “I should go.”

“You could.”

He studied her face for fear, for triumph, for the tremor of someone making a threat she wasn’t prepared to carry out. He found none.

“What do you want?” he asked.

“To understand how it feels.”

“How what feels?”

“To hear the knock.”

She glanced toward the front hall, as if someone might be standing there.

Martin’s pulse beat once, hard, in his throat. “You’re not making sense.”

“I know.” She stood. “It’s difficult to explain a thing you’ve spent years pretending isn’t happening.”

He moved toward the door. She didn’t block him.

That was the worst part.

At the threshold, he turned back. “You think you know what I am.”

“I do.”

“And what are you?”

For the first time, something changed in her expression. Not fear. Not anger. Grief, perhaps—old and carefully folded away.

“I’m the person who opened the door,” she said.

Martin’s hand went to the knob.

From somewhere deeper in the house came a soft knock.

He froze.

The woman looked past him. “There it is.”

Another knock. Patient. Polite.

Martin stared at her. “Who’s that?”

“I don’t know,” she said. “But I imagine you do.”

The front door was still closed. No one could have knocked from inside the house.

A third knock sounded, this time from the sitting-room window.

Martin backed away from it.

The woman picked up her teacup. Her hand was perfectly steady.

“You’ve spent a long time choosing people who were alone,” she said. “You must have wondered what it would be like to meet someone who wasn’t.”

Outside, a shadow crossed the rain-streaked glass.

Martin looked at the woman. “You’re a killer.”

“Yes.”

The word fell between them without drama.

“How many?”

She lifted the cup to her lips. “Enough to know that numbers don’t make a person feel less alone.”

The knocking began again—front door, window, somewhere upstairs. Not loud. Not urgent. Just the same small, courteous sound, repeated through the house.

Martin backed toward the hall.

The woman stayed where she was.

“You could come with me,” he said.

She smiled faintly. “I’ve been waiting for you to say that.”

And then, from the darkness at the end of the hall, a voice called Martin by his real name.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: A shapeshifting alien was sent to Earth at the dawn of humanity and has been a bystander for every major event . He is now returning home and is asked to judge the human race .
content:
### The Witness

When the ship found him, it was waiting above the blue edge of the world.

For the first time in six thousand years, Namar had no human face.

He stood in the ship’s silver chamber as the shape he had been born with: a narrow, translucent body, its bones shining like moonlit water. The crew regarded him with their dark, unblinking eyes.

“You have observed them from their beginning,” said the captain. “You have seen what they become. We ask you to judge the human race.”

Namar looked down at Earth.

“I will answer,” he said.

He had been sent there when humans were few, when the nights were cold and the dark held teeth. His instructions had been simple: observe, record, do not interfere.

So he had watched.

He had worn the face of a woman beside the first fire, while a child reached toward the flames and learned that warmth could be held. He had been a man with a broken spear when a hunter, rather than keep his food, divided it among the injured. He had sat at the mouth of a cave as someone painted the animals they feared and loved, as though the world might vanish unless it was remembered.

He had watched villages become cities. He had watched kings raise monuments to themselves, and strangers raise walls against one another. He had stood in crowds as people shouted the names of their gods, their rulers, their enemies. He had seen each generation invent new ways to kill—and new words for why the killing was necessary.

Once, in a city of stone, he had carried water to a man dying beneath a cross. He had not known then whether the condemned man was a prophet, a rebel, or simply unlucky. He knew only that the soldiers were tired, that one of them had a blister on his heel, and that the man on the cross had asked them to forgive one another.

Namar had not intervened.

He had watched plagues empty streets. He had watched ships cross oceans carrying both wonder and chains. He had watched the first machines rise, the first bombs fall, and the first footprints press into the dust of another world.

At the edge of a ruined city, he had seen a little girl place a flower in the hand of a dead stranger.

He had recorded that, too.

For six thousand years, he had made himself whatever shape the moment required: soldier, servant, teacher, mourner, passerby. He had learned to imitate their laughter. He had learned that grief changed the face more than age did. He had learned that humans could look at the same fire and see a hearth, a weapon, or a warning.

“You were sent to assess their fitness for contact,” the captain said. “Their violence is extensive. Their divisions are persistent. Their survival has depended upon the suffering of others.”

“Yes,” said Namar.

“And yet you hesitate.”

“I do.”

The captain’s eyes narrowed. “Why?”

Namar looked back at Earth. Clouds moved across it, white and gentle from this height. Beneath them were forests burning, cities waking, hospitals crowded, kitchens lit. Somewhere, someone was choosing whether to tell the truth. Somewhere else, someone was choosing not to.

“Because they are not finished,” he said.

“No species is finished.”

“Most species do not spend their brief lives arguing over what they ought to be.”

The chamber was silent.

Namar remembered a boy sitting alone beside a river, making a small boat from bark. The boy had set it afloat, watched it catch in the reeds, and waded into the cold water to free it. He had no reason to save the boat. He had made it, and that had been enough.

He remembered a woman holding the hand of her enemy in a hospital corridor, both of them waiting for the same child to come through the doors.

He remembered the first time humans looked back at their planet from space. Their voices had gone quiet. They had called it beautiful. For a moment, the whole world had fit inside a window, and they had understood that nothing divided them from the people below—not borders, not banners, not the old names for enemies.

They had understood.

They had forgotten.

Then remembered again.

“Do you judge them innocent?” asked the captain.

“No.”

“Then guilty?”

Namar considered the word. He had heard it spoken in courts and bedrooms, in temples and trenches. Humans used it as if it were a door that could be closed.

“They are guilty,” he said. “Of cruelty, of cowardice, of looking away. They are guilty of knowing what pain is and making it for one another anyway.”

The captain inclined his head. “Then your judgment is clear.”

“No,” said Namar. “That is only part of it.”

He watched the sun rise over the curve of Earth. Even from orbit, the morning looked like a promise no one had earned.

“My judgment is that they have not yet become what they are capable of becoming.”

“That is not a verdict.”

“It is the only honest one.”

The captain turned toward the others. “And what sentence do you propose?”

Namar thought of the child at the fire, of the flower in the dead man’s hand, of the tiny boat freed from the reeds. He thought of every moment when humans had been terrible, and every moment when they had chosen, against habit and fear, to be something else.

“Another morning,” he said.

The captain stared at him. “You would grant them more time?”

“I would not grant it. They already have it.”

“And if they fail?”

“Then they will have failed with the knowledge that they could have done otherwise.”

Namar stepped toward the ship’s window. Below, dawn spread over the planet, touching oceans, rooftops, forests, and fields without distinction.

For the first time in six thousand years, he allowed himself to hope that a human might look up and see him.

Then he turned back to the council.

“Let them be judged again,” he said, “when they have had the chance to choose.”
