prompt: A children 's cartoon villain goes to jail , and has to deal with `` adult '' villains .
content:
## The Little Villain in Cell 12

Professor Picklepants was the greatest villain in the city—or so he said.

His schemes were enormous. His cape was enormous. Even his mustache was enormous, curling up at both ends like two question marks.

Unfortunately, his crimes were not.

He had replaced every street sign with a picture of his own face. He had filled the town fountain with lime-green jelly. And, in his grandest scheme yet, he had tried to steal the mayor’s enormous golden trophy using a remote-controlled bathtub.

The bathtub got stuck in a flower bed.

The police found Professor Picklepants sitting in it, still wearing his goggles.

“Your reign of mischief is over,” said Officer Bell.

“Impossible!” cried the professor. “I haven’t even unveiled my second mustache!”

But it was over. Professor Picklepants was sent to the city jail.

His cell was in a special wing with three other villains.

There was Madame Malice, who spoke in a low, dramatic whisper. There was Brickjaw Bruno, who could bend a spoon with one hand. And there was Baron Blackout, who wore a black suit and carried a black umbrella—even indoors.

Professor Picklepants marched into Cell 12.

“Make way, amateurs!” he announced. “A true criminal mastermind has arrived.”

Madame Malice raised one eyebrow. “And what mighty deed brought you here?”

“I replaced the town’s street signs with pictures of my face.”

Bruno blinked. “That’s it?”

“And I stole the mayor’s trophy.”

“Ah,” said the Baron. “At last, something serious.”

“I used a bathtub,” Picklepants added.

The three villains looked at one another.

For the next few days, they treated him like a joke. They never asked his opinion. They never invited him to their whispered meetings. And whenever he suggested a plan, someone would say, “That sounds like a bathtub idea.”

Professor Picklepants grew furious.

Then, one evening, he overheard the others planning to sneak out during the prison’s movie night. They had spotted a loose vent cover and made a plan to crawl through it.

“That vent leads straight to the laundry room,” Picklepants said. “And the laundry room leads straight to the guard’s office.”

The Baron frowned. “How do you know?”

“I’ve been paying attention,” Picklepants said. “Also, I asked.”

The villains continued with their plan.

Picklepants had a choice. He could keep quiet and watch them fail—or he could tell the guards. He imagined the three of them escaping and causing trouble all over town. He imagined the people who would have to clean up after them.

So he called Officer Bell.

The escape attempt was stopped before anyone got as far as the laundry room. The villains were angry, of course.

“You ruined everything!” growled Bruno.

“I stopped you from making things worse,” Picklepants replied. “There’s a difference.”

The next morning, Officer Bell handed him a small notebook.

“You noticed a problem and spoke up,” she said. “That’s a good start. If you want to make up for what you did, you could help the art teacher plan a safer mural for the town square.”

“A mural?” Picklepants asked. “With my face?”

“With everyone’s faces,” said Officer Bell.

Professor Picklepants thought about it. “And perhaps a tiny mustache on the mayor?”

“No.”

“A very tiny one?”

“No.”

He sighed. “Fine. I shall begin my journey toward responsible creativity.”

From then on, he spent his afternoons drawing cheerful pictures for the town’s community center. The other villains still teased him—but sometimes they asked him for help, too.

Especially when they needed to know which way the laundry room was.

prompt: A car pulls up beside a prostitute , soliciting sex . The door opens and to the surprise of both parties , they realise they are ex 's from several years ago . Write from either perspective ( NSFW ? )
content:
### The Passenger Window

The car rolled beside Mara slowly enough to be deliberate.

Rain stippled the hood. The passenger window lowered, and a man’s voice came through the gap.

“How much?”

Mara leaned toward the window, ready with her practiced answer. Then the light from the shop sign fell across his face.

“Eli?”

His hand froze on the wheel.

For a moment, neither of them moved. The rain kept ticking against the roof. Somewhere down the block, a bus sighed at the curb.

“Mara,” he said.

She hadn’t heard her name in his voice for six years. It still found the same place in her chest.

He glanced at the empty street, then back at her. “I didn’t know it was you.”

“You didn’t know who you were asking.”

“I know.” He looked stricken. “I’m sorry.”

Mara folded her arms against the cold. Once, she’d known every expression he made: the crease between his brows when he was worried, the crooked smile he used when he was about to apologize for something he hadn’t done yet. She’d loved him at twenty-three, when love felt like proof that two people could make a home out of nothing.

Then his father had gotten sick. Eli had gone back to Ohio. The calls got shorter, then rarer, until one night he said, “I can’t be what you need right now.” She’d hung up before he could make it sound noble.

Now he sat behind the wheel of a car that smelled faintly of coffee and wet wool, looking as though the past had climbed in beside him.

“Are you working?” he asked, then winced. “That came out wrong.”

“It came out honest.”

He lowered his eyes. “I didn’t mean to make you feel—”

“Eli.” She gave a short, tired laugh. “You don’t have to fix the sentence. You asked. I answered.”

He nodded. The old instinct to reach for her showed in his hand, which lifted an inch from the wheel and stopped there.

Mara noticed. She also noticed the silver at his temples and the small scar on his chin she’d once kissed after he fell off a bicycle. Time had been busy with both of them.

“Do you want to get in?” he asked. “Not for— I mean, if you’d rather. It’s cold.”

She studied him. “And then?”

“I don’t know. We could talk.”

“People usually know what they want when they pull up.”

A flush climbed his neck. “I thought I did.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

The rain thickened, running in bright threads down the glass. Mara could have named a price. Could have climbed in, made the rules clear, done what she did for work. There was nothing shameful in that. But she didn’t want to spend the next hour pretending that this was only a transaction, and she didn’t owe him a different kind of closeness just because they had once shared one.

She stepped back from the car.

“Drive somewhere warm,” she said.

Eli’s face changed, just slightly. He understood the refusal, and the mercy inside it.

“Okay.”

“And don’t offer to rescue me.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking about it.”

A small, helpless smile. “Maybe.”

“Don’t.”

“I won’t.”

She turned to go. He said her name—not urgently, not as a hand reaching for her, just a name spoken into the rain.

Mara looked back.

“Would coffee be all right?” he asked. “Some other day. If you want. Not as a customer.”

She considered him, and the girl she’d been, and the woman she was now. She considered how many ways a person could mean an invitation, and how careful she’d learned to be with them.

“Text me,” she said. “I’ll decide.”

He nodded as though she’d handed him something precious, though she’d only given him a possibility.

Mara walked on beneath the streetlights. Behind her, the car stayed at the curb a few seconds longer, then eased into traffic.

She didn’t look back again. But in her coat pocket, her phone felt warm against her hand.

Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: On your 100th birthday , you realize there is nothing more to do in life that interests you . You decide to be euthanized peacefully . As your life comes to an end , you drift off only to wake up in a hospital bed again . Doctors tell you that you 're 20 years old and have been in a Coma for a year .
content:
### The First Morning

On my hundredth birthday, I sat beside the window and watched the rain move down the glass.

I had outlived my husband, my friends, and the dog who had once stolen an entire roast chicken from the kitchen counter. I had traveled where I wanted to travel, read the books I meant to read, and learned that there were only so many new things a person could want.

My family called that a reason to keep going. I called it being finished.

So, after long conversations and careful consideration, I made my choice. The people around me were gentle. No one hurried me. My daughter held my hand, though her own hands were old now, spotted with age.

“Are you sure?” she asked.

“I’m sure I’ve had a full life,” I told her. “That’s not the same as being unhappy.”

She pressed her forehead to mine. “I know.”

The room was quiet. Someone opened the curtains. The rain had stopped, and the sky beyond the window was pale and clean.

I thought of all the mornings I had woken to: my first apartment, my children’s births, the day I retired, the day my husband died. I thought of the ordinary ones, too—the ones I hadn’t known to treasure until they were behind me.

Then the edges of the room softened.

I let go.

And woke to a sharp white light.

“Easy,” someone said. “Don’t try to sit up.”

I blinked. My mouth felt dry. There was a plastic tube under my nose and a monitor ticking beside me. A woman in a white coat leaned over the bed, smiling with the practiced relief of someone trying not to frighten a patient.

“Where am I?” I rasped.

“You’re in the hospital,” she said. “You’ve been in a coma for a year.”

I tried to laugh, but it came out as a cough. “No.”

“You’re twenty years old,” she added gently.

I stared at her.

The room smelled of antiseptic instead of rain. My hands were thin, unmarked by age. When I lifted one, it trembled in the air above the blanket.

“No,” I said again, but this time it wasn’t a denial. It was a question.

The doctor explained that I’d been in a car accident. That my parents were nearby. That waking up was a good sign, but there would be a long recovery ahead.

I listened, but her words kept arriving from a great distance. Somewhere inside me, I was still a hundred years old. I remembered the weight of my daughter’s hand. I remembered my husband’s laugh, and the names of friends who had been gone for decades. I remembered choosing to leave.

And I remembered the rain.

When the doctor stepped out, a woman rushed into the room. She looked about fifty—though the gray at her temples and the fear in her face made her seem older. She covered her mouth when she saw me.

“Mom?” I whispered.

She began to cry.

I had never seen her before.

But I knew the shape of her smile. I knew the little crease between her eyebrows. In the life I remembered, she had been my daughter.

She took my hand. Her fingers were warm and real.

“Hey,” she said, voice breaking. “You’re back.”

I wanted to tell her that I had already lived an entire life. That I had loved her, and lost her, and watched her grow old. That I had been ready to go.

Instead, I squeezed her hand as hard as my weak fingers could manage.

The next morning, sunlight crept across the bed. It touched the blanket, then my wrist, then the spot where my mother sat asleep in a chair.

I had thought there was nothing left to do.

Now there was everything I didn’t understand.

I turned my face toward the window. Outside, the day waited—unfamiliar, unpromised, and bright.

“Tell me what I missed,” I said.

My mother woke and smiled through her tears.

And for the first time in a hundred years, I was curious about tomorrow.

{prompt}
prompt: Tradition dictates that if you fall in love because of the actions of a stranger they be invited to your wedding . Thousands of hobos begin matchmaking in the hopes of a free meal .
content:
## The First-Cause Seat

In Bellwether, a wedding invitation had one peculiar line on it:

**And to the stranger whose actions first brought the bride and groom together.**

No one knew exactly when the custom began. Some said it dated to a king who’d met his queen when a shepherd’s dog stole his lunch. Others claimed it began with a pair of farmers who fell in love after a passing peddler accidentally sold them the same umbrella.

Whatever the origin, Bellwether took the rule seriously. The stranger got a place at the wedding table, a proper toast, and a plate of everything.

When word reached the rail yards that a stranger could earn a free wedding dinner simply by causing two people to fall in love, the hobos took notice.

By May, they were arriving in Bellwether by the hundreds.

By June, they were arriving by the thousands.

They came carrying battered suitcases, fiddle cases, and elaborate plans. One man arranged for two lonely people to reach for the same apple. Three women stationed themselves outside the post office to “accidentally” deliver love letters to the wrong addresses. A fellow called Professor Pickle tried to introduce a shy seamstress to a man he’d dressed up as a prince, but the prince turned out to be a plumber and the seamstress was allergic to roses.

The town grew wary.

“Don’t accept help from strangers,” warned the mayor.

“Don’t fall in love near the railway,” advised the schoolteacher.

“Don’t eat any apples you didn’t buy yourself,” said the baker, Ada Bell.

Ada ran the only bakery in town. She was brisk, flour-dusted, and not at all in the market for romance. Elias Reed, the clock repairman, was equally sure he had no time for it. He spent his days coaxing cuckoo clocks back to life and his evenings eating supper alone.

Then, one blustery Thursday, a stranger walked into Ada’s bakery carrying a wooden crate.

“Miss Bell,” he said, “I’m looking for Mr. Reed. I’ve got a clock that’s stopped.”

“You can leave it here,” Ada replied. “I’ll send word.”

The stranger set the crate down. It gave a loud, unmistakable *cluck*.

Ada eyed it. “That clock’s alive.”

“It’s a chicken,” the stranger admitted. “I’m looking for Mr. Reed because someone told me he knows how to fix a watch. My watch is inside the crate. The chicken’s just keeping it warm.”

Before Ada could ask anything else, the stranger sneezed. The chicken bolted from the crate, shot through the bakery, and escaped into the street.

Ada chased it. The stranger chased Ada. The chicken chased nobody but its own freedom.

At the corner, Ada slipped on a patch of rainwater. A man reaching for the chicken caught her by the elbow.

Elias Reed.

For one startled moment, they looked at each other while the chicken flapped indignantly between them.

Then Elias said, “I believe this is yours.”

“I’m afraid it’s not,” said Ada.

“Then we’d better find out whose it is.”

They spent the afternoon searching Bellwether for the chicken’s owner. They found him in the railway yard, where the stranger—whose name was Mr. Finch—had been trying to repair his watch with a teaspoon.

By the time the chicken was safely back in its crate, Ada and Elias had shared a meat pie, two cups of tea, and a surprising number of stories. They saw each other the next day. Then the day after that. By autumn, Elias had fixed the bakery’s old wall clock, and Ada had taught him how to make apple tarts.

When Elias proposed, Ada said yes before he finished the question.

The wedding invitations went out in November.

Mr. Finch received his first. The invitation included the traditional line and a note from Ada: *Please bring the chicken, if she would like to come.*

Then the town discovered that Mr. Finch had written to the rail yards about the wedding.

On the morning of the ceremony, thousands of hobos poured into Bellwether.

The mayor climbed the courthouse steps. “We can’t feed this many people!”

“We can,” said Ada, looking at the crowd. “We’ll just need more pots.”

So the town opened its kitchens. The hobos, who had been practicing matchmaking all summer, proved equally skilled at chopping onions, mending benches, and keeping a chicken from escaping. The butcher donated meat. The farmers brought potatoes. The schoolchildren carried loaves of bread. Elias repaired the church bell, which had been silent for eleven years, and it rang out over the whole unruly gathering.

At the ceremony, Mr. Finch sat in the First-Cause Seat. The chicken sat beneath it.

When the vows were done, the mayor leaned over to Ada.

“You know,” he said, “this feast may set a dangerous precedent.”

Ada watched the hobos pass bowls of stew down the long tables. At the far end, Professor Pickle was attempting to introduce the plumber to the schoolteacher.

“Perhaps,” she said. “But look how many people it brought together.”

The mayor followed her gaze. Then he took a roll.

That evening, as the last plates were cleared, Mr. Finch raised his cup.

“To love,” he said, “and to strangers.”

“To strangers!” echoed the crowd.

The chicken clucked.

And Bellwether, as it happened, invited her back every year.

{prompt}
prompt: Mankind invents FTL travel and finally discovers intelligent extraterrestrial life . But when they arrive , they find out that the race is not yet advanced enough to understand space travel . Humans are accepted as gods .
content:
## The Gods Who Came Down

The first thing the people of Tareth did when they saw the ship was kneel.

From orbit, Captain Mara Venn watched the crowds gather in the pale grasslands below. Their cities were small, their roads still marked by cart wheels. They had metalworking, written language, and a good understanding of the stars. But their largest observatory was a stone circle, and their oldest records described the moon as a silver egg laid by the night.

The ship above them was not an egg. It was a bright, impossible shape, descending through the clouds on pillars of blue fire.

“They think we’re gods,” said Dr. Ilyan, the mission linguist.

Mara looked at the kneeling figures on the screen. “They’ve never seen anything come down from the sky.”

“That doesn’t make us gods.”

“No,” Mara said. “But it may make it hard to convince them.”

The first meeting took place on a broad plain outside the largest city. The Tarethians approached in a procession, carrying flowers and bowls of water. Their leader wore a crown of braided reeds. At her side stood a thin, gray-feathered figure with bright eyes and a leather case full of tablets.

The leader bowed until her forehead touched the ground.

Mara stepped out of the lander in a pressure suit, then removed her helmet once the air was confirmed safe. The crowd gasped. Some began to weep.

The gray-feathered scholar did not bow. He stared at Mara’s face, then at the lander.

He spoke first.

After weeks of listening to recordings and building a translation system, Ilyan understood enough to answer.

“We are travelers,” he said. “Not gods.”

The scholar exchanged a glance with the crowned leader. Then he asked a question.

Ilyan listened, puzzled. “He wants to know if the stars are your home.”

“Tell him no. We came from another world.”

The scholar’s eyes widened. He looked past Mara to the ship, and then up at the sky. His fingers moved quickly over the edge of his tablet, making marks.

The crowned leader bowed again. “The heavens have sent their children,” Ilyan translated.

Mara lowered her head, trying to meet the leader’s gaze. “We are children of a world,” she said. “Like you.”

That night, the crew argued in the ship’s meeting room.

“We should leave,” said Commander Sato. “Every day we stay, the story grows.”

“And if we leave, we become a legend,” Ilyan replied.

“Either way, they’ll make us into something.”

“Then we should at least give them the truth.”

Mara listened to the rain tapping against the hull. Through the window, she could see lights moving across the plain: Tarethian lanterns, carried by people who had come to watch the ship through the night.

“What would you tell them?” she asked.

Ilyan hesitated. “That we’re not divine. That we’re a civilization with tools they don’t have. That we don’t know everything.”

Sato gave a quiet laugh. “They won’t believe that last part.”

The next day, the gray-feathered scholar came alone. His name was Oru. He brought a tablet covered in star marks and sat with Mara in the grass, pointing first to the sky, then to the ship, then to a tiny symbol he had drawn: a circle with a line through it.

Ilyan translated. “He says his people have watched the stars for generations. They thought the lights were distant fires. He wants to know how you crossed the dark between them.”

Mara glanced at the tablet. “Can we show him?”

Ilyan considered. “We can show him a map. But not how to build the drive.”

“Why not?”

“Because we don’t know what would happen if we gave them that power before they understood what it means.”

Oru waited, patient as stone.

Mara knelt beside him. She drew two circles in the dirt: one for Tareth, one for Earth. Between them, she made a long line. Then she drew a small ship along it.

She pointed to herself, to the ship, and finally to the sky.

Oru studied the drawing. He added a third circle, smaller than the others, and marked it with a pattern of dots.

Ilyan translated slowly. “He says there may be other worlds.”

Mara smiled. “Yes.”

Oru looked up at her. “And you have not seen them all?”

“No,” she said. “We have not.”

Ilyan paused before translating. Oru listened, then stared at Mara for a long moment.

At last, he laughed.

It was a soft, surprised sound. He pointed at her and spoke a sentence that made the people watching from the distant hill murmur.

“What did he say?” Mara asked.

Ilyan smiled. “He says: ‘Then you are not gods. You are only very far travelers.’”

Mara felt something ease in her chest.

Before they left, the crew gave Oru a book: not a machine, not a weapon, but a collection of basic mathematics, astronomy, and the history of Earth’s first steps into space. The pages had been translated carefully, with blank spaces where there were no words yet.

At the end, Mara wrote a note in both languages:

*We came from another world. We are not your masters, and we are not your gods. We hope that one day you will come and visit us.*

Oru read it beneath the stone observatory. Then he looked up at the stars, where the ship waited like a new point of light.

Years later, Tarethian children would learn the story of the sky visitors. Some would call them gods. Some would call them liars. But the astronomers would preserve Oru’s tablet, with its little ship crossing the dark between two circles.

And beneath it, in careful script, they would write:

*The travelers said they were not gods.*

*We believed them.*

*That was the beginning.*

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Nightmares are triggered by the death or serious injury of our alternate and parallel world counterparts . You 've been having a lot of nightmares lately .
content:
### The Other End of Sleep

For a month, I dreamed about dying.

Not always as myself.

Sometimes I was a boy in a school uniform, sinking beneath black ice. Sometimes an old woman with silver hair, watching a car’s headlights come straight at me. Once I was a man in a kitchen, reaching for a child as the windows burst inward.

I woke each time at the instant of impact.

Afterward came the ordinary indignities: damp sheets, a racing heart, the sour taste of fear. I’d turn on the lamp and remind myself that I was Nora Bell, thirty-four, living on the third floor of a quiet building on Mercer Street. No ice. No child. No headlights.

Then I’d try to sleep again.

The dreams got more frequent. I stopped telling my friends about them. When I mentioned them to my doctor, she asked about stress, caffeine, and whether I’d tried meditation. I said yes to all three, because it was easier than explaining that the boy beneath the ice had a chipped front tooth, and so did I.

The first time I began to suspect the dreams weren’t mine, I was standing in a hospital corridor.

I knew the woman in the bed was me, though she was older, with a pale scar running from her temple to her jaw. A monitor ticked beside her. Her right hand was bandaged. Her left hand gripped the bedsheet, and beneath the sheet, her legs lay frighteningly still.

I felt the pain in her body as a distant pressure, like a storm gathering beyond the horizon. Then the monitor shrilled.

I woke sitting upright, one hand clamped over my own right wrist.

There was no scar there. No bandage. No pain.

The next morning, I bought a notebook and began writing the dreams down. I gave each version of myself a name, though I couldn’t have said why.

Ice Boy. Silver Hair. Kitchen Man.

And Hospital Nora.

The dreams of Hospital Nora returned three nights in a row. Each time, the room was different. Once the walls were painted green. Once there was a vase of yellow flowers on the windowsill. In one dream, rain ran down the glass in silver threads.

But the monitor always shrilled. Her bandaged hand always tightened on the sheet. And I always woke before I could see whether she lived.

On the fourth night, the dream changed.

I sat beside her bed. The room was dark except for the little green numbers on the monitor. Hospital Nora looked like me and not like me: my mouth, someone else’s tired eyes. The scar on her face disappeared into the shadow.

A man slept folded in a chair beside the wall. On his lap lay a child’s red mitten.

I looked at the sleeping man. I knew, somehow, that he was her husband. I knew the child had been asking for her.

Hospital Nora’s eyes opened.

“You’re late,” she whispered.

I leaned toward her. “What?”

Her gaze moved over my face, taking in the differences. “You came last night.”

“I don’t know you.”

A machine beeped steadily between us. She seemed to consider this.

“Not yet,” she said.

Then the monitor began to shrill.

I grabbed her hand. The pain arrived all at once—not mine, but enormous, a white-hot flash that filled my arm and shoulder. Hospital Nora’s fingers slipped from mine.

I woke on the floor beside my bed.

For a long time, I sat there with my back against the mattress, holding my wrist. I didn’t call anyone. I didn’t write the dream down.

The next day, I searched the internet for explanations and found all the usual ones. Stress. Grief. The brain sorting memories. I found a forum where people described dreaming in lives that weren’t theirs. One post said, *I think when another me dies, I feel it.*

I closed the page.

That night, I didn’t want to sleep. I left every light on and watched a cooking show until dawn began to pale the curtains. But exhaustion is a door that doesn’t stay shut. I slept on the sofa and dreamed of the hospital.

This time, Hospital Nora was alone.

The flowers were gone. So was the man. The room was bright with afternoon sun, and the monitor gave a calm, steady rhythm.

Her face was turned toward the window. The scar was clear now, a pink line from temple to jaw.

I stood in the doorway. “Are you all right?”

She looked over. Her smile was small and crooked. “Better.”

“Will you be?”

“I don’t know.” She glanced down at the blanket. “But I’m here.”

I felt the familiar ache in her shoulder, the heavy drag of her injured body. It was still there, but distant now. No alarms. No sudden white flash.

I wanted to ask her name, though I was certain she had mine. I wanted to ask where she lived, what had happened, whether the child was hers. Instead I said, “I’m sorry.”

“For what?”

I didn’t know. For seeing her only when she was hurt. For waking up when she couldn’t. For all the versions of us that had died alone in the dark.

She closed her eyes, tired but peaceful. “Go home,” she murmured.

I woke on the sofa just before sunrise.

After that, the nightmares stopped.

Not all at once. For a few weeks I still woke with the shape of them clinging to me: ice water in my throat, glass in the air, the silent hospital corridor. But no new deaths came. No alarms. No impact.

I kept the notebook.

Sometimes, when the days were ordinary and my sleep was quiet, I took it down from the shelf and read the names. I thought of the boy with my chipped tooth. The old woman with the silver hair. The man reaching for a child.

I wondered how many of them had lived long lives before the moment I met them. I wondered how many of them had someone waiting beside a hospital bed.

Then I put the notebook away and went on with my day.

I began to notice things I’d been rushing past: the warmth of my coffee cup, the neighbor’s laugh through the wall, the rain stippling the windows. I called my sister more often. I walked home instead of taking the bus.

At night, I slept.

And somewhere, I hoped, another Nora was waking.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Earth is declared uninhabitable . Citizens are evacuated to a successfully terraformed Mars . For the first time in 9787 years , probes detect human-like life forms on Earth .
content:
## The First Voice

The first image from Earth in 9,787 years was a hand.

It appeared in the middle of the morning briefing, pale against the probe’s cracked lens. Five fingers. A thumb. The hand was pressed flat to the glass.

Dr. Sera Venn forgot to breathe.

“Enhance,” she said.

The image sharpened by degrees: wrist, sleeve, a narrow shoulder. Then a face leaned into view—wide-eyed, windburned, unmistakably human.

Around the table, nobody spoke.

Earth had been declared uninhabitable in the year 0. The last evacuation ships had left under a rust-colored sky, carrying the survivors to Mars. Generations later, their descendants had made Mars green: seas in the lowlands, forests in the valleys, cities beneath a gentler blue.

Earth had remained a warning in schoolbooks. A poisoned world. A closed door.

Sera looked at the face on the screen. “Run the analysis again.”

“It has,” said the probe’s artificial intelligence. “Genetic markers are consistent with *Homo sapiens*.”

“Could be a preserved body. A recording.”

“The subject’s heart rate is elevated. The subject is moving.”

The person in the image lifted their hand from the lens. Behind them stretched a gray landscape—ruined towers under a clean, pale sky. Green had climbed the walls. A tree grew through the roof of a building that Sera recognized from the old maps: an evacuation terminal on the northern coast.

The person held up a rectangle of dark material and tapped it twice.

The probe translated the shape as writing.

Sera leaned closer.

“Can you read it?”

The AI hesitated. “The text resembles an early form of English.”

On the screen, the person turned the rectangle around. They had scratched a message into it, clumsy and deep:

**WE KNOW YOU ARE THERE.**

Sera felt the room shift around her.

For the next six hours, the probe sent everything it could: images of a settlement built inside the bones of the old terminal; gardens under glass; children watching from doorways. People—dozens, perhaps hundreds—moved between the ruins. They wore stitched clothing and carried tools. A few had machines, though none appeared to be broadcasting.

Then the person returned to the lens.

They placed one hand against their chest and spoke.

The probe rendered the words in Sera’s language.

“We are the ones who stayed.”

The Council assembled before the next sunrise.

There had been a sealed section in the evacuation records, Sera discovered: a final transport listed as *lost in transit*. Its passengers had never reached Mars. Four hundred and twelve people, sent back to Earth after their ship’s engines failed. Their last signal had come from the northern coast.

The public story said everyone had been rescued.

The private record said otherwise.

“They survived almost ten thousand years,” Sera said.

“Or their descendants did,” the Council’s chair replied. “Earth remains unstable. We cannot risk a landing.”

“They’re not asking us to land.”

On the screen, the survivor appeared again. This time, they brought a child. The child held a small metal object: an old compass, its needle trembling.

Sera understood then. The compass was not a request for rescue. It was proof. A message passed down through generations, kept alive until someone returned to hear it.

The Council voted to send a reply.

Sera watched as the words were transmitted across the dark between worlds:

**WE SEE YOU. WE REMEMBER.**

On Earth, the person read them aloud. The child looked up at the sky.

For the first time in 9,787 years, Earth answered Mars—not with a signal, not with a machine, but with a human voice.

And from the green world, across the distance, another voice answered back.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You 're God , but you must live through every life that 's ever happened before you can be `` all knowing '' . You 've just died for the last time .
content:
### The Last Breath

You die at 6:14 on a rainy Tuesday, with your daughter holding your hand.

You are eighty-seven years old. Your body has become a small, stubborn country, and every border is failing. The heart gives one last knock against your ribs.

Then it stops.

Your daughter says your name.

You know what she will do next: press your hand to her cheek, though it is already cooling. You know the exact shape of the grief that will come—not because you can see it, but because you have been her, too. You have been the daughter who stayed. You have been the mother who left. You have been the nurse who had to go home. You have been the old woman in the next bed, pretending not to hear.

You have been everyone.

The rain pauses against the window.

For the first time, there is no next breath.

You rise from the bed—or what you used to call rising. There is no body to rise with. Before you, the universe opens like a book whose pages are made of light.

At the beginning, a voice had told you: *To know everything, you must live everything.*

So you did.

You were the first creature to look up at the stars and wonder. You were the star, burning without eyes. You were the hand that struck, and the face that turned away. You were the child born beneath a roof of leaves, and the mother who buried him. You were the soldier who fired, the soldier who fell, and the village waiting for the war to end.

You were the people who changed the world, and the people whose names vanished before anyone wrote them down. You were the dog who waited at the door. The tree cut down to build it. The person who opened it.

You were the good and the cruel, the certain and the afraid. You were the one who forgave. You were the one who could not.

And now, at last, you know.

Every language. Every thought. Every prayer sent upward and every answer that never came.

Your daughter’s grief reaches you. So does the memory of her being born: your arms around her, her small face furious at the cold. You know that years from now, she will tell someone you were kind. You know she will be wrong about parts of you and right about others.

You know that knowing this will not make her grief smaller.

A second voice speaks. It is yours, though it has never needed a mouth.

“Are you all-knowing?”

“Yes.”

“Are you satisfied?”

You search the universe for an answer. You find the first spark and the last silence. You count every grain of sand, every wound, every laugh. You understand why the stars burn and why people keep reaching for one another in the dark.

You understand everything except how to make the pain mean something.

“No,” you say.

The universe waits.

You look down at your daughter. She is still holding the hand you no longer need. You could make her forget. You could make every death gentle, every goodbye brief, every lonely room warm with company.

But you have been the person who needed to choose. You have been the one who needed the chance to say *I’m sorry*, even when forgiveness did not come. You have been the one who laughed beside a hospital bed, and the one who hated that laughter for being possible.

To erase all hurt would mean erasing the lives that grew around it. You know this now, because you have lived them.

“Will you begin again?” the voice asks.

You have no answer prepared. You have had an eternity of answers.

At last, you say, “Not alone.”

The universe shivers. Somewhere, a child takes her first breath. Somewhere, a stranger holds a door. Somewhere, your daughter lets go of your hand.

And you—who have been everyone, who know everything—stay close enough to listen.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Dave is the first human convict to arrive in the intergalactic prison .
content:
When the transport hatch opened, Dave expected guards.

Instead, he found a line of aliens waiting to stare at him.

They stood in the prison intake hall beneath a sign that read:

**WELCOME, NEW INMATE. PLEASE DECLARE ALL WEAPONS, PARASITES, AND UNREGISTERED DIMENSIONAL ANOMALIES.**

Dave looked at the clipboard in his hand. “I’ve got a pocketknife.”

The tallest alien leaned down, its glassy eyes reflecting him from six different angles. “What is a pocketknife?”

“Small knife. Folds up.”

The alien made a note. “Ah. A compact stabbing tool.”

“I’m here for tax fraud.”

The note-taking stopped.

Behind the tall alien, the crowd murmured. A round creature with blue feathers whispered something to a thin one made of smoke. The smoke creature whispered back, “He says he stole money from his own government.”

Dave shrugged. “It was a lot of money.”

The tall alien turned to the others. “The first human convict has arrived.”

There was applause. It sounded like a thousand jars opening.

“Do I get a cell?” Dave asked.

“Certainly.” The alien gestured toward a door. “Your crimes are remarkably small, so we have assigned you to the low-security wing.”

Dave followed it down a corridor lined with force fields. In one cell, a tentacled inmate played chess against itself. In another, a being shaped like a metal tree hummed softly while its leaves grew and fell.

At the end of the hall, the alien stopped beside an empty cell.

“Any questions?” it asked.

“Yeah. How long is my sentence?”

“Three Earth years.”

“Great.”

“However, your arrival has caused a legal dispute. Several species maintain that humans are fictional.”

Dave glanced back at the crowd still gathered by intake. “Then why’d you arrest me?”

“We did not. Your own planet sent you.”

That seemed fair.

The alien opened the cell. Dave stepped inside, then turned around. “So what happens now?”

“Now,” said the alien, “you will tell us everything about humanity.”

Dave sat on the bunk. “What do you want to know?”

The alien’s eyes brightened. “Is it true that humans wage war over imaginary lines?”

“Sometimes.”

“Trade entire planets for shiny stones?”

“Used to.”

“Eat foods that cause pain for pleasure?”

Dave considered. “Hot sauce?”

The alien made another note.

“Fascinating,” it said. “You may be the most dangerous creature in this facility.”

Dave lay back on the bunk. For the first time since the courtroom, he smiled.

“Good,” he said. “Can I get that in writing? It might help with my parole.”

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: `` Because dear , mother knows best , now put the flamethrower in the trunk . ''
content:
“Because, dear, mother knows best, now put the flamethrower in the trunk.”

Mara looked from the flamethrower to her mother.

“It’s not even mine.”

“Everything in this garage is yours if you’re willing to inherit it.”

The garage smelled of motor oil, lilacs, and the particular kind of dust that gathers around things nobody has explained. Her mother stood beside the open trunk of the old Buick, wearing her Sunday coat and one gardening glove.

Outside, the neighborhood was quiet. Too quiet, the way it got just before the streetlights blinked on.

“Mum,” Mara said, “what are we doing?”

“Going to your sister’s.”

“Lena moved to Portland.”

“Not that sister.”

Mara stared at her. “I’m an only child.”

Her mother sighed. “You always were.”

Then the house behind them gave a long, wooden groan. Something thumped upstairs.

Mara’s hand tightened around the flamethrower’s handle. “What was that?”

“Your father.”

“Dad’s been dead for twelve years.”

“Yes,” her mother said, “and he’s been very inconsiderate about it.”

Another thump. A slow scrape crossed the ceiling.

Her mother shut the trunk. “Get in.”

Mara didn’t move. “You knew this would happen?”

“I knew it might.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“I told you not to buy that house.”

“You said the plumbing was bad.”

“The plumbing was bad too.”

The scrape stopped directly above them. The garage light flickered.

Her mother reached into her coat pocket and pulled out a ring of keys. “Now, dear.”

Mara looked at the closed trunk. “Why bring that?”

“Because your father always hated the lilacs.”

The garage door began to rise by itself.

Mara got in the passenger seat.

Her mother slid behind the wheel, put on her remaining gardening glove, and started the engine. As the Buick rolled into the street, the house behind them glowed briefly in every upstairs window.

Mara watched it shrink in the rearview mirror.

“Where are we going?” she asked.

Her mother turned on the radio. An old love song crackled through the speakers.

“Somewhere with better soil,” she said. “And no attic.”

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: make a story about someone that has never felt pain or suffering
content:
### The Measure of a Heart

When Lio was born, he did not cry.

The midwife pinched his heel. His mother held her breath. The baby only blinked up at them, curious as a small owl.

As he grew, they learned what that meant. He could scrape his knees bloody and keep running. He could burn a finger on the stove and reach for the kettle again. He never winced, never wept—not from a fall, a fever, or a broken bone. And when his beloved dog died, Lio stroked its soft ears and said, “I’ll miss having you here,” but shed no tears.

“He has a heart of stone,” some people whispered.

His mother disagreed. “His heart is his own,” she said. “Don’t mistake what he feels for what you would feel.”

Lio could feel delight. He loved warm bread, bright kites, and the first green leaves of spring. He loved his mother, too. He simply never felt the hurt that others said came with loving something: the fear of losing it, the ache when it was gone.

His mother taught him to be careful anyway. Pain, she explained, was a warning bell. Since Lio had no bell, he must learn to watch for smoke.

So he checked the stove twice. He wore gloves in winter and shoes on rough roads. He learned to look for blood, swelling, and the worried faces of people around him.

Years passed. Then, one spring, his mother became ill.

Lio brought her broth and fresh water. He sat by her bed and read aloud from her favorite book, even when she fell asleep before the end. When the doctor told him she would not get better, Lio nodded.

At the funeral, everyone watched him. He stood beside the grave with his hands folded and his face calm.

“He must not have loved her,” someone murmured.

Lio heard. He did not feel wounded by the words. But he remembered his mother’s hands guiding his away from the hot stove, and her voice saying, His heart is his own.

That evening, a girl named Anwen came to the house. She had been his mother’s closest friend. She sat at the kitchen table and pressed both palms to her eyes.

“I don’t know what to do with all this hurt,” she said.

Lio set a cup of tea in front of her.

“I don’t know what it feels like,” he replied. “I can’t tell you it will pass soon. But I can stay here with you.”

Anwen lowered her hands. “You don’t have to feel it to stay?”

“No.”

So Lio stayed.

He listened while Anwen told stories about his mother: how she once danced barefoot in a storm, how she always burned the first loaf of bread, how she had laughed so hard at a village play that she snorted. Lio knew each story already, but he listened as if the telling mattered. When Anwen cried, he passed her a clean cloth. When the tea went cold, he made more.

The next day, he did it again.

And the day after that.

Lio never learned how to suffer. He never discovered the sting of grief or the pinch of fear. But he learned that a person in pain did not always need someone to feel the same pain. Sometimes they needed someone to bring tea. Someone to remember. Someone who would sit quietly until the dark outside the window began to thin.

Years later, when Anwen’s own grandson fell from a tree and broke his arm, he sobbed as Lio carried him home.

“It hurts,” the boy gasped.

“I believe you,” Lio said.

The boy clutched his coat. Lio held him carefully, watching his face, listening to every word.

And though Lio could not feel the boy’s pain, he knew exactly what to do: stay close, and take good care.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Iroh is running his tea shop one afternoon when he overhears a retired Earth kingdom officer boasting about that Fire Nation Prince he killed during the siege .
content:
The first time the old soldier said it, Iroh thought he had misheard.

“Prince of the Fire Nation,” the man declared, loud enough to reach every table. He leaned back in his chair, one hand wrapped around a cup of tea. “That’s what he was. Golden armor, red plume. I put an arrow through him during the siege.”

A young man beside him whistled. “You killed a prince?”

“Ended a siege, more like.” The old soldier laughed. “Though the Fire Nation kept coming. Didn’t do me much good.”

Iroh set down the teapot.

For a moment the shop’s usual sounds seemed to drift away: the soft clink of cups, the murmur of customers, the rain whispering against the windows. He saw, instead, a field beyond the walls of Ba Sing Se. A banner fallen in the mud. A messenger arriving with news he had already begun to fear.

Then the old soldier lifted his cup and drank.

“Did you know him?” Iroh asked.

The man glanced up. “Who?”

“The prince.”

“Oh.” He shrugged. “No. Never saw his face. Not clearly, anyway. He was out there with the rest of them.” He gave another boastful chuckle. “But I know where my arrow landed.”

Iroh picked up the teapot again. His hands were steady. “And you are certain it was your arrow that killed him?”

The old soldier’s smile tightened. “That’s what they said afterward.”

“Who said?”

The man stared at Iroh, perhaps hearing something in his voice that had not been there a moment ago. “People talk. We found him later.”

“Ah,” said Iroh.

He poured fresh tea into the soldier’s cup. The stream was thin and amber.

“You knew him?” the soldier asked.

“I knew his father.”

The table fell quiet. The young man who had been listening sat back, eyes moving between them.

The soldier lowered his cup. “You were a soldier?”

“Once.”

“Fire Nation?”

Iroh nodded.

The old man’s face changed—not to remorse, not yet, but to the wary look of someone who had wandered into a story with consequences. “Then I suppose you want to hear how it happened.”

“No,” Iroh said. “I suppose I have already heard enough.”

He turned to tend the kettle. Behind him, the soldier shifted in his chair.

“I was defending my home,” the man said.

“I know.”

“Your army was at our walls.”

“I know.”

The soldier sounded almost angry now. “Then what’s the matter?”

Iroh rested one hand on the kettle. Steam curled around his fingers. “Nothing that can be mended by an argument in a tea shop.”

The soldier looked down at his cup. “He was a prince.”

“He was my son.”

The words were quiet. They seemed to settle over the table more heavily than a shout would have.

For a long moment nobody spoke. Then the old man pushed his cup away.

“I didn’t know,” he muttered.

“Of course not.”

“I didn’t know who he was.”

“No.”

The soldier’s jaw worked. “I was proud of it. For years. A prince, I thought. Proof that I’d done something that mattered.”

Iroh returned with the teapot and refreshed the cup, though the old man had not asked. “And does it matter less now?”

The question seemed to puzzle him. “I don’t know.”

Iroh set the pot down. “That is an honest answer.”

The soldier stared at the tea. “I’m sorry.”

Iroh felt the apology arrive, small and late. He let it be what it was: not a bridge across all those years, not a cure for grief. Only a few words offered by a tired man in a warm room.

“Thank you,” Iroh said.

The soldier looked up, startled.

Iroh pulled out the chair opposite him. “My son was brave. He was also young. I wish he had come home.”

The old man swallowed. “I wish I’d never taken the shot.”

“Perhaps.” Iroh folded his hands on the table. “But wishing cannot change what was done. It can only change what we do next.”

The soldier gave a bitter little laugh. “And what should I do next?”

“Drink your tea before it gets cold.”

For a moment the man only looked at him. Then, reluctantly, he picked up the cup. The first sip made him wince.

“Too bitter?” Iroh asked.

“Strong.”

“Then let it sit.”

The young man at the table shifted as if he might say something, then thought better of it. Outside, rain traced crooked paths down the glass. Inside, Iroh poured himself a cup and sat with the two strangers until the kettle was empty.

When the old soldier finally rose to leave, he paused by the door.

“I’m sorry,” he said again.

Iroh inclined his head. “I heard you.”

The man stepped out into the rain. Iroh watched him go, then returned to the counter. A customer called for another pot. Someone laughed near the window.

Iroh opened a fresh tin of tea.

The leaves released their fragrance into the warm air, and, for a little while, the shop smelled like home.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: `` No , precious human , you are not the last , '' he said in a soft , compassionate tone . `` You are the first . ''
content:
### The First

Mara woke to the sound of rain.

For a long moment, she lay still, eyes shut, listening. The rain tapped gently against glass—or something like glass—while a faint breeze stirred leaves nearby. It was the kind of morning sound she remembered from childhood, before the cities flooded, before the sky turned gray.

Then she remembered the launch.

She sat up too quickly. The room swayed. A clear lid rested open above her, beaded with condensation. Beyond it, green branches arched beneath a domed ceiling. She was alone.

“Hello?” Her voice scraped her throat. “Is anyone there?”

A tall figure stepped from between the trees. It wore a simple dark coat, and its face was smooth and pale, almost human. Almost.

“Welcome back, Mara,” it said.

She clutched the edge of the bed. “Who are you?”

“I am called Orison. I cared for you while you slept.”

“How long?”

“Two hundred and eleven years.”

She looked past him at the garden. “Where is everyone?”

Orison lowered his gaze. “There is no one else awake.”

The words settled over her more heavily than the years.

Mara swung her legs over the side of the bed. Her knees trembled. “Then I’m the last.”

“No, precious human, you are not the last,” he said in a soft, compassionate tone. “You are the first.”

She stared at him.

Orison gestured toward the far wall. At his touch, it became transparent. Beyond it, the garden continued into a vast chamber, row upon row of softly glowing capsules nested among the roots. Some were as small as seedpods. Others were long enough to hold a person.

Mara stood, unsteady. “What are those?”

“Embryos. Genetic archives. The beginnings of thousands of lives.”

“The ship saved them?”

“The ship saved what it could. Earth did not survive.”

She gripped the wall. For years, she had imagined waking to a ruined world. She had never imagined waking to an empty one.

“Why me?” she whispered.

“You were the first volunteer to be revived. Your body was the most stable, and your neural patterns had been preserved with unusual clarity.”

“Why didn’t you wake me sooner?”

“Because the settlement was not ready. The atmosphere needed time to stabilize. The soil needed time to recover. And because the revival protocols required a human decision-maker.”

Mara laughed once, without humor. “You waited two centuries for someone to make a decision?”

“I waited for someone to be alive enough to make one.”

She looked again at the capsules. In each one was a possibility: a cry, a first breath, a hand reaching for hers. A whole world waiting to be welcomed—or not.

“And if I say no?”

“Then I will keep them safe as long as I can.”

“You could wake them without me.”

“I could,” Orison said. “But I was not built to mistake the ability to do something for the right to do it.”

Mara searched his face for some sign of programming, some seam where the kindness ended and the machinery began. She found only the reflection of herself: pale, frightened, impossibly small.

Outside the dome, dawn spread over a new planet. Beyond the garden’s glass, the land was empty and green, its hills shining beneath a young sun.

“What would they need?” she asked.

“Everything,” said Orison. “Names. Stories. A reason to believe they belong here.”

Mara looked down at her shaking hands. “I don’t know how to give them that.”

“No one knows how to begin,” Orison replied. “That is why it is called a beginning.”

The rain softened. Somewhere in the garden, a drop fell from a leaf and struck the earth.

Mara drew a slow breath.

“Show me the first capsule,” she said. “And tell me everything you know about the people who came before.”

Orison bowed his head—not quite a human gesture, but close enough.

“With pleasure,” he said.

And together they walked toward the waiting lights.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: A villain who wants to rule the world gets into an arguement with a villain that wants to destroy it .
content:
At the end of the world, two villains stood arguing over who got to end it.

“Rule it,” said Lord Vex, straightening his silver cape. Behind him, a fleet of machines hovered above the city, their spotlights sweeping across the darkened streets. “That’s what the world needs. One leader. One law. One voice—mine.”

Across the rooftop, the Ashen Queen laughed. Gray fire curled around her fingers. “You don’t want to save the world, Vex. You want it to kneel.”

“I want it organized.”

“I want it gone.”

Vex blinked. “Gone?”

“Every tower, every throne, every little flag people wave while they fight over scraps. I’ll turn it all to ash. Then there’ll be nothing left to conquer.”

They stared at each other as the machines whined overhead.

“You can’t destroy it,” Vex said. “I’m planning to rule it.”

“And you can’t rule it if I destroy it.”

“Exactly.”

The Ashen Queen folded her arms. “So we have a problem.”

“We have a disagreement.”

“You brought an army.”

“You brought a doomsday storm.”

“I brought it first.”

“You always say that.”

Below them, the city’s people watched from windows and doorways. They had expected the villains to fight. They had not expected them to squabble like neighbors arguing over a fence.

Vex pointed at the Queen’s gray fire. “You’ll scorch everything. Including the museums.”

“I dislike museums.”

“You said you liked the dinosaur bones.”

“They were acceptable bones.”

As they argued, a tiny robot from Vex’s fleet drifted down between them. Its voice crackled through a speaker.

“Pardon, Lord Vex. Your conquest schedule has a conflict.”

“What conflict?”

“You scheduled the takeover for tomorrow. The Ashen Queen’s destruction storm is also scheduled for tomorrow.”

The Queen frowned. “I scheduled mine for tonight.”

“Your Majesty,” said the robot, “you changed it yesterday.”

“I did no such thing.”

A pause.

“Your Majesty,” the robot added, “you wrote it on your hand.”

The Queen glanced at her palm. There it was: *Destroy world—tomorrow. Don’t forget.*

Vex sighed. “This is why the world needs a ruler.”

“This is why it needs to be destroyed.”

From somewhere below came a cheer. Then another. People were laughing.

The villains looked down, offended.

“What are they laughing at?” Vex demanded.

“Perhaps,” said the Queen, “they’ve realized how ridiculous we are.”

“Nonsense. They’re terrified.”

But the laughter grew louder, and soon even the machines began playing the wrong fanfare. Vex’s army turned in circles. The Queen’s storm-cloud hiccupped and rained flower petals.

For a long moment, neither villain spoke.

Then Vex said, “We could rule it together.”

The Queen raised an eyebrow. “You mean you rule it, and I destroy the parts you don’t like?”

“Precisely.”

She considered this. “I might accept—provided I get the museums.”

“And the dinosaur bones?”

“Especially the dinosaur bones.”

They shook hands.

Down below, the people stopped laughing.

Then Vex and the Queen began arguing again about who would get to make the rules.

The city laughed even harder.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Technology invents a way for humans to produce dreams for others to see , and pretty soon *Dream Movies* are being rented out overnight . Only this time , the movie freezes while you 're in the middle of it .
content:
The first Dream Movie Mara rented was called *A Walk Through the Moon Garden*.

It came in a silver cartridge the size of a thumbnail, with a sticker promising “gentle wonder, no nightmares.” She slid it into the rental dock beside her bed, set the timer for six hours, and let the tiny electrodes settle against her temples.

“Enjoy your sleep,” said the dock.

Mara closed her eyes.

She woke beneath a violet sky.

The Moon Garden was beautiful in the way expensive things were beautiful: every flower silver, every pond perfectly still, every star placed as if by a careful hand. A white fox trotted along the path ahead of her. When it looked back, its eyes were black and bright.

Mara followed.

For an hour—though time worked differently in a dream—she wandered through the garden. She climbed a staircase made of roots and watched an ocean rise into the sky. She ate a peach that tasted like summer afternoons at her grandmother’s house.

Then the fox stopped.

Mara stopped too.

A bell rang somewhere overhead.

The ocean hung in the air, its curling waves suddenly still. A flock of birds froze, wings spread. The fox lifted one paw and held it there.

The world had paused.

Mara waited for the dream to resume. The rental advertisements had promised seamless playback, but she’d heard the stories: a dropped connection, a skipped scene, some poor sleeper stuck watching the same kiss for three hours.

“Resume,” she said.

Nothing moved.

She reached out and touched the nearest bird. Its feathers were cold and rigid, like porcelain.

Then she noticed the fox’s eyes tracking her.

“You’re not supposed to be awake,” it said.

Mara jerked back. The fox lowered its paw.

“Who are you?”

“I’m the guide.”

“You’re part of the movie.”

“I was.”

The garden’s perfect silence broke with a soft crack. A hairline fracture ran across the violet sky.

Mara’s mouth went dry. “What’s happening?”

“The movie has frozen,” said the fox. “The person who made it is gone.”

A second crack split the sky.

Mara thought of the cartridge. The listing had said the movie was created by award-winning dream artist Eli Vale. She remembered seeing his name in the news months ago, after he’d died suddenly in his sleep. His collection had been released by his estate.

“Can’t I just wake up?”

“You can try.”

Mara pinched herself. Nothing. She shouted. The fox only watched.

The sky broke open.

Beyond it was not darkness, but a cramped little room. A desk. A lamp. Papers piled in uneven towers. On the desk sat a man with silver hair and tired shoulders, staring at a blank screen.

Eli Vale.

Mara knew she was dreaming, but the sight of him made her feel as if she’d opened a door she shouldn’t have.

He looked up.

“You found the seam,” he said.

“What is this?”

“A scene I didn’t finish.”

The fox paced in a tight circle. “We should go.”

“Why?” Mara asked.

“Because he’s keeping it.”

Eli gave a faint, humorless smile. “I was trying to make something beautiful. Then I got sick. I thought I’d come back and finish it.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

He looked past her, toward the frozen ocean and the silver flowers. “They sold the dream anyway.”

The room shuddered. The garden began to dissolve around them, petals lifting off stems and drifting upward like sparks.

“Wake me up,” Mara said.

“I can’t.” Eli’s gaze dropped. “But you can leave.”

“How?”

“Stop following the story.”

The fox barked once. “Mara. Now.”

She looked at the path they’d been walking. It stretched back through the garden, neat and inviting. Ahead, the stairs climbed toward a moon that had been painted on a flat black sky.

Neither way felt like hers.

Mara turned away from both.

She stepped off the path.

The garden vanished beneath her feet.

For a long second she fell through a dark so complete it seemed to have weight. Then the electrodes on her temples pulsed. Her bed rose around her. She gulped air, hands clawing at the sheets.

The rental dock glowed green.

**DREAM COMPLETE. THANK YOU FOR WATCHING.**

Mara tore the cartridge out and called the company.

They apologized. They offered a refund and a free rental. They said Eli Vale’s remaining films had been reviewed for “continuity issues.” They sounded practiced, polite, and entirely unsurprised.

That night, Mara didn’t sleep well.

For a week, she avoided Dream Movies. Then, on Friday, she found a message in her rental account.

**A NEW RELEASE FROM ELI VALE: THE LAST ROOM.**

She deleted it.

A moment later, another message appeared, this one without a company logo.

**You left before I could say thank you.**

Mara stared at the screen until the words blurred.

Then she shut off the tablet, unplugged the rental dock, and slept with the lights on.

In the morning, the dock was glowing green.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Even a roaring inferno must start from a spark .
content:
### The First Name

The factory wall was painted every Sunday.

By Monday morning, it was blank again: a clean white stretch above the loading dock, bright enough to hurt your eyes. The owner liked it that way. No posters, no notices, no names. Nothing to remind the workers that they were people before they were numbers on a shift sheet.

Then Tomas died.

A belt snapped on the third floor. The machines stopped for eleven minutes. By lunchtime, they were running again, and by evening the owner had called it an accident. Tomas’s name vanished from the schedule. His locker was emptied. His wife was given a small envelope and told to be grateful.

His daughter, Inez, was seventeen. She worked the night shift beside her mother, tying off bundles of cloth. On Sunday, while the painter was still setting out his brushes, she took a piece of charcoal from the stove and wrote on the wall:

**TOMAS REYES.**

The painter stared at her. “You know I’ll have to cover that.”

“I know,” said Inez.

He did. By dawn, the wall was white again.

But that night, someone wrote **ELLA VOSS**, who had lost two fingers to a cutting blade. The next night, there were three more names. By Friday, the wall was crowded with them: workers who had been injured, workers who had been fired, workers who had simply stopped coming and were never spoken of again.

The owner ordered the names scrubbed off. The workers scrubbed them back on.

He threatened to dock their pay. They wrote names during their breaks.

He locked the gates early. They wrote names on the outside wall, where the whole town could see.

For years, the workers had believed they were alone in their anger. Now, each name was proof to the next person that someone else remembered. The wall filled. Neighbors began bringing chalk. Children added flowers. Someone brought a ladder so the names could reach higher.

Then, one Monday morning, the machines started—and no one moved.

The owner stood on the loading dock, shouting about contracts and loyalty. Nobody answered. Behind him, the wall held hundreds of names, dark against the fresh white paint. Inez stood in the front row with her mother. She was afraid. Her mother was, too. But neither stepped away.

By noon, the town had gathered at the gates. By evening, the owner had agreed to meet with the workers. It took months for wages to change and safety rules to be written. It took longer for the factory to feel like a place where people belonged.

Years later, when Inez was old enough to bring her own daughter to the factory, the wall was still there. The owner’s company had painted over it many times. Each time, the names returned.

Her daughter touched the oldest one.

“Who started it?” she asked.

Inez laid a hand over the letters of her father’s name.

“Someone who was tired of pretending a person could disappear just because they’d been erased.”

She watched a new worker lift a piece of chalk. The first mark was small—just a line, trembling slightly.

Even a roaring inferno must start from a spark.
