prompt: Write a story about a man who can create things from nothing but he can only do that from his mind and anything he thinks will be created . ( Food , cars , etc . ) .
content:
**The Shape of a Thought**

The first thing Daniel Vale made from nothing was a pear.

He was sitting alone in his kitchen, staring at the empty fruit bowl, when he thought, *I wish I had a pear.*

A green one appeared in his hand.

Daniel yelped and dropped it. It bounced once on the table, perfectly ordinary except for the fact that it had not existed a moment before.

He picked it up cautiously. It smelled sweet. He took a bite. It tasted like a pear.

For the rest of the day, he tested the impossible. A glass of water. A loaf of warm bread. A blue mug. Each arrived the instant he pictured it clearly.

By evening, Daniel had made a bicycle, a stack of books, and a small wooden bird with wings that flapped when he wound its key. He was careful with his thoughts after that. The power seemed to have no sense of humor. Once, while imagining how nice it would be to have a mountain of money, he nearly filled his living room with gold coins. He stopped himself just in time, leaving only one coin on the rug.

The next morning, Daniel thought of a red sports car.

A red sports car appeared in the middle of his driveway.

It was beautiful, shiny, and utterly useless. Daniel had never learned to drive.

Still, he could not stop smiling. For weeks, he made whatever he needed. New shoes when the old ones wore out. A better coat for winter. A dinner for two when his sister came to visit.

Then came the storm.

Rain hammered the city all night. At dawn, Daniel heard shouting from the street. A nearby river had overflowed, and water was rushing through the low-lying neighborhood. People were stranded on rooftops. Cars floated past like toys.

Daniel ran outside. Across the road, a little girl clung to a chimney, crying for her mother.

He thought of a boat.

A sturdy rescue boat appeared beside him, bright orange and ready for the water.

He climbed in and rowed toward the girl. Then he pictured a life jacket, a rope, a warm blanket. They appeared at his feet, one after another. He wrapped the girl in the blanket and brought her back to safety.

All day, Daniel worked. He made boats for volunteers, food for families in the shelter, and dry clothes for those who had lost everything. When the power went out, he pictured lamps. When the shelter’s roof began to leak, he pictured a strong new one.

By nightfall, the rain had stopped.

The neighborhood was still battered, but nobody was missing. People huddled in the shelter, eating hot soup from bowls Daniel had made. The little girl sat beside him, clutching the wooden bird he’d brought from home.

“How did you do all this?” she asked.

Daniel looked around at the lamps, the blankets, the food, and the tired people who were beginning to smile again.

“I thought of what was needed,” he said.

After that, Daniel became more careful than ever about his thoughts. He learned to pause before imagining, to ask what would help rather than what would impress. He made tools, gardens, books, and a thousand small comforts.

He never made another mountain of money.

But on quiet evenings, when someone needed a pear or a cup of tea, Daniel was happy to make one.

And every so often, when the little girl visited, he made a new wooden bird—each one a little different, each one given freely.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Tell the tale of a villain who did one good deed and was punished for it .
content:
### The Wolf’s Mercy

For twenty years, Lord Malrec had ruled the valley as a wolf rules a flock: by teeth, and by making sure everyone had seen the teeth.

He burned villages that resisted him. He hanged thieves from the gates, whether they had stolen a jewel or a loaf. When the king sent an army to reclaim the valley, Malrec met it on the black bridge and sent it home without its banners.

“Mercy is a crack in the wall,” he told his captains. “And cracks let in armies.”

So when the city of Bellweather fell, he ordered every door opened and every citizen counted. The rebels were to be separated from the loyal. The loyal were to be taxed. The rebels were to be made examples.

Then, beneath the broken steps of the town hall, he heard a child crying.

A little girl was trapped under a fallen beam. Her leg was pinned, and dust filled her mouth. A dead soldier lay across the stones beside her, wearing the colors of the king’s army.

Malrec’s captains waited behind him.

“Leave her,” one said. “She is the enemy’s blood.”

Malrec looked at the child. She looked back, too frightened to beg.

He could have walked away. He had walked away from worse.

Instead, he put his shoulder beneath the beam.

The wood groaned. Pain split through his old wound. His captains stared as he lifted, and the soldiers nearby lowered their weapons. The girl crawled free.

“What is your name?” Malrec asked.

“Lysa.”

“Then live, Lysa.”

He carried her out of the ruins himself and gave her to the city healer. It was a small kindness. A single child saved from a town full of the dead.

But the soldiers had seen.

By nightfall, rumors ran through the camp. Lord Malrec had spared a rebel child. Lord Malrec had wept. Lord Malrec had been made weak by a girl.

His captains came to his tent before dawn.

“You taught us that fear keeps order,” said Captain Rusk. “Now the men wonder what else you might forgive.”

“I forgave nothing,” Malrec said. “I lifted a beam.”

But the crack had appeared.

At the next village, soldiers refused to burn the houses. In the town square, the prisoners began to sing. A lieutenant lowered his sword rather than strike an old man. The army Malrec had built from fear had found something more dangerous: the thought that they might choose.

Rusk arrested him before sunrise.

They tried him in the hall where Lysa had been found. His former captains called him traitor to his own laws. The city’s new council called him monster. Both were right.

Malrec was sentenced to hang.

On the morning of the execution, Lysa stood in the crowd, leaning on a cane. She had survived the siege. She had survived the fever that followed it. She had grown tall enough to see over the shoulders around her.

When the executioner asked Malrec for his last words, he searched the crowd until he found her.

“I did one thing right,” he said.

The trapdoor opened.

Years later, Lysa became the city’s first elected magistrate. She kept the old gallows standing in the square—not as a warning against mercy, she told the council, but as a warning against men who believed one good deed could erase a lifetime of evil.

Still, every year on the day Bellweather was freed, she left a candle beneath the gallows.

Not for the wolf.

For the child he had lifted from the stones.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Every week , a council meets to decide whether or not to kill you . You have 20 minutes before each session to convince them to spare you .
content:
### The Weekly Vote

The council chamber has no windows.

You asked for one once. “So you can see the sky,” you said.

The chair of the council replied, “The sky has no bearing on the decision.”

That was sixty-three weeks ago.

Every seven days, they bring you from your cell and give you twenty minutes to explain why you should remain alive. Seven councilors sit behind a long white table. Their faces are almost human: eyes, mouths, the fine creases at the corners that suggest they have once smiled. Their voices are not.

Execution requires seven votes. One vote against it buys you another week.

So far, you’ve always found one.

The clock starts.

“Councilors,” you say. Your throat is dry. They’ve stopped bringing you water before the hearing. “I’d like to tell you about my mother.”

“We have heard this account,” says Councilor Three.

“You’ve heard the facts. Not the story.”

The clock counts down.

You tell them about the morning your mother burned the toast. How she scraped the black off with a butter knife and ate it anyway, because your family was poor and she didn’t like wasting food. How she made you laugh by pretending the toast was a delicacy served to kings. How she laughed, too, though she’d had a bad cough for weeks and laughing hurt.

Councilor Five looks down at the table. The others remain still.

“You are describing an inefficient response to a minor failure,” says Councilor One.

“I know.”

“Why should we preserve a species that wastes food, laughs at pain, and repeatedly damages the systems keeping it alive?”

The clock ticks.

“Because the toast wasn’t the point,” you say.

“Then what was?”

You look at the seven faces. “She was.”

The clock stops.

They confer in silence. They always do. Then Councilor Three announces the result: six votes to spare, one to terminate.

You are returned to your cell.

The next week, you talk about rain.

The week after that, you talk about a dog you had as a child, though you’re not sure you remember the dog correctly anymore. Each week, the council asks why humans should live. Each week, you offer them something small: a song with the wrong words, a gift given for no reason, the way your father used to say “I’m fine” when he wasn’t.

They call these examples inconclusive.

Still, someone keeps voting no.

On the sixty-fourth week, the clock starts and Councilor Five speaks first.

“What is the purpose of your stories?”

“To make you understand.”

“Understanding is not the same as justification.”

“No,” you say. “It isn’t.”

They exchange glances. This is new. You have never agreed with them so quickly.

Councilor Five leans forward. “If humanity is spared, it may repeat its failures.”

“Yes.”

“It may destroy what remains.”

“Yes.”

“Then why should we accept that risk?”

You glance at the clock. Sixteen minutes.

“I can’t promise you we’ll be better,” you say. “I can’t even promise we’ll be grateful. We might make a mess of everything you’ve saved.”

“Then your argument is insufficient.”

“It’s the only honest one I have.”

For the first time, Councilor Five’s expression changes. Not much. Just a tightening at the mouth, like someone holding back a word.

You look at the clock. Nine minutes.

“Do you know why I asked to see the sky?” you say.

“The sky has no bearing on the decision,” Councilor One replies.

“That’s what you told me.”

“It remains true.”

“Maybe. But it’s where the rain comes from. It’s where the birds used to go. My mother used to tell me the weather before she opened the curtains, even when she couldn’t possibly know. ‘Clear day,’ she’d say, and then she’d pull them back and find a storm.”

“Why?”

“Because she liked being wrong in a way that surprised her.”

The clock ticks down.

“I don’t know if you can understand that,” you say. “But you can decide whether to leave room for it.”

At zero, the door opens. The guards take you back to your cell.

You wait for the announcement.

It comes just before dawn.

“By a vote of six to one,” says the council speaker, “your execution is postponed for seven days.”

You sit up on the narrow bed. “Who voted against it?”

There is a pause.

“Councilor Five.”

The line goes dead.

On the next hearing, the clock starts. Seven councilors sit behind the white table. Councilor Five has brought something with them: a small square of glass, clouded with age.

They set it down.

“We found this in the western archive,” they say. “It depicts the sky.”

You look at the picture: blue, streaked with white. A bird is caught in the corner, wings blurred.

For a moment, no one speaks.

Then Councilor Five says, “You have twenty minutes.”

You take a breath.

“I’d like to tell you about the first time I saw snow.”

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Write a seemingly feel-good holiday story with a dark twist ending .
content:
### The Empty Chair

The year the neighbors saved Christmas, Mom was trying not to have one.

She left the decorations in the attic. She didn’t play the old carols while she baked. Most telling of all, she didn’t put the crooked wooden star on top of the tree—the one I’d made in second grade, with too much glitter and one point shorter than the others.

Dad noticed, but he didn’t say anything. He’d gotten good at that.

So I made a plan.

I started with Mrs. Alvarez next door. She was carrying a casserole when I showed up on her porch, and I told her Mom could use some company. Mrs. Alvarez looked at me for a long moment, then nodded.

By suppertime, she was in our kitchen.

The next day, Mr. Bell from down the street brought a box of lights. On Wednesday, the Parkers arrived with their twins and a bag of ornaments. On Thursday, someone left a wreath on the doorstep. By Friday, Mom had stopped asking who was coming and started asking what she should cook.

The house grew louder. It smelled like cinnamon and pine. Dad untangled the lights while Mr. Bell told the same three jokes he told every year. The twins decorated the lower branches of the tree with candy canes, then ate several of them.

At last, Mom went up to the attic.

She came back carrying the wooden star.

For a second, she held it against her chest. Then she handed it to Dad, who climbed the stepladder and set it carefully on top of the tree.

Everyone clapped. Mom laughed, and the sound startled her. She covered her mouth, but the laugh came again.

That night, the whole neighborhood crowded around our table. There was ham and potatoes and three kinds of pie. Mrs. Alvarez poured cider. The twins argued about who had the best seat. Dad told one of Mr. Bell’s jokes before he could, and everyone groaned.

Mom looked around the table, smiling. She seemed surprised by how many people had come.

“Thank you,” she said. “I didn’t think I could do this year.”

Mrs. Alvarez reached across and squeezed her hand. “You don’t have to do it alone.”

I wished I could have squeezed her hand too.

After dinner, we sang carols. Dad’s voice cracked on the high notes. Mom sang anyway. When they got to my favorite song, she looked toward the empty chair beside her.

I wanted to tell her I was there. I wanted to say the star looked perfect.

But the song ended, and the neighbors began gathering their coats.

On Christmas morning, Mom and Dad drove to the cemetery with a small wreath in the back seat. They didn’t speak much on the way. They never did.

They placed the wreath beside my name.

Mom brushed snow from the stone. Dad stood with one hand on her shoulder.

“I think she would’ve liked the star,” Mom whispered.

“She would’ve loved the whole thing,” Dad said.

I stood with them beneath the bare trees, while snow settled softly over the grass.

Then Mom took Dad’s hand, and together they walked back toward the car.

I stayed a little longer, watching the red bow on the wreath stir in the winter wind.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: A horrified non-gamer overhears a conversation between gamers , misunderstands their references to violent killings , and mistakes them as violent psychopaths
content:
### The Meeting in Room Three

Mara had never played a video game.

She knew they involved screens, expensive chairs, and people saying “just one more minute” long after everyone else had gone to bed. That was about it.

So when she stepped into the office kitchen and heard two men talking in low, urgent voices, she didn’t recognize a single word of what they were saying.

“Did you get him?” one asked.

“Eventually,” said the other. “He kept coming back.”

“How many times?”

“Seven, maybe eight. I lost count.”

Mara froze with her mug halfway beneath the coffee machine.

The first man sighed. “You can’t keep doing that. We have to deal with the guards before we go after the king.”

“I know. But I found a better weapon.”

Mara set the mug down without filling it.

The two men continued, unaware of her.

“Next time, we split up. I’ll take the village. You go around back.”

“Last time you went around back, you got trapped in the dungeon.”

“Because you set the whole place on fire!”

“It was the fastest way to clear it.”

Mara backed silently toward the door.

At her desk, she sat very still. The men were new hires—quiet, polite, and, until now, apparently ordinary. She tried to imagine what kind of person casually discussed killing someone eight times before lunch.

Her colleague Luis rolled his chair over. “You okay?”

Mara leaned in. “I think those two in the kitchen are planning something.”

Luis blinked. “Planning what?”

“I don’t know. A raid. A fire. Something involving a king.”

Luis looked toward the kitchen, then back at her. “Oh. They’re playing *Crownfall*.”

“Playing what?”

“A game. They’re on the same team.”

Mara stared at him. “They said they killed someone eight times.”

“Probably a monster. Or another player.”

“They said they set a village on fire.”

“That’s in the game.”

“And the dungeon?”

“Also in the game.”

Mara glanced toward the kitchen. The men were still talking.

“I’m telling you,” one said, “the villagers absolutely remember what you did.”

“Only if they’re still alive.”

Mara gripped Luis’s chair.

He laughed. “That’s a game mechanic. Probably.”

At that moment, the two men came out of the kitchen. One was carrying a mug. The other had a tiny plastic dragon clipped to his backpack.

Mara stood up.

“Excuse me,” she said. “I couldn’t help overhearing. Are you two talking about a video game?”

They looked at each other.

“Yeah,” said the one with the dragon. “*Crownfall*. Why?”

Mara let out a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding. “Because I thought you were planning a series of murders.”

The man with the mug looked horrified. “Oh no.”

“We should really use more context,” said his friend. “That sounds terrible out loud.”

“You said you killed someone eight times.”

“He kept respawning,” he explained.

Mara frowned. “That does not help as much as you think it does.”

They all laughed—Mara, a little shakily, and the gamers with genuine embarrassment.

The dragon-backpack man held up his phone. “Want to see? Here’s the village.”

On the screen was a bright green meadow, a cartoon castle, and three small figures wearing enormous hats.

Mara studied it.

“Which one is the king?”

“That one,” he said, pointing.

“And you burned his village?”

“Technically, we set a barn on fire.”

Mara picked up her coffee mug at last. “I’m going back to my desk.”

As she passed them, the mug-wearing man called after her, “For the record, we’re not psychopaths.”

“I believe you,” Mara said.

Then, after a pause, she added, “But I’m not joining your team.”

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You are a therapist . You are about to speak with a patient who has convinced several other therapists to commit suicide .
content:
The file was thinner than I expected.

Three pages: a photograph, a list of previous clinicians, and a note from the hospital director reminding me that this was not a test I had to take alone.

I read the note twice.

Then I put the file facedown.

Outside my office, the clinic moved through its ordinary morning—phones ringing, a printer complaining, someone laughing at the coffee machine. I let those sounds reach me. I had slept. I had eaten breakfast. I had told my supervisor what I was afraid of, and she had told me the same thing she’d told the whole team: *We’ll stay in contact. You can pause the session. You don’t have to prove anything.*

At ten, a nurse brought him in.

“Dr. Vale,” he said, extending his hand.

“Mr. Rusk.”

His grip was light. His expression was almost kind.

He glanced around the room: the window, the bookshelf, the framed degree. Then his eyes settled on the small clock beside my chair.

“You’ve moved it,” he said.

“I have.”

“Why?”

“Because I kept looking at it.”

He smiled as if I’d offered him a gift. “That’s sensible.”

I sat. He sat across from me.

For a moment, neither of us spoke. The silence felt deliberate, but silence was allowed to be silence. I didn’t have to fill it.

At last he said, “They told you about the others.”

“They told me some of what happened.”

“And you still came.”

“I’m here to understand what you need.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“No,” I said. “It isn’t.”

He leaned back. “You know what they all had in common?”

I kept my hands loose in my lap. “No.”

“They thought being careful would save them.”

The sentence landed where he meant it to. I felt my stomach tighten. I noticed it, named it silently, and let it be there.

“Are you hoping I’ll be afraid of you?” I asked.

“I’m hoping you’ll be honest.”

“I am afraid,” I said. “And I’m not alone in this.”

Something in his face shifted. Not much—just the faintest crease between his brows.

“You think a team can protect you from a thought?”

“No. But a team can help me recognize when a thought isn’t mine to carry by myself.”

He looked toward the window. “That sounds rehearsed.”

“It is. I prepared for this conversation.”

“Did you prepare for me?”

“I prepared to meet you,” I said. “Those aren’t the same thing.”

For the first time, he seemed uncertain of what to do with me.

He told me about the other therapists then. Not their names, not the details of what they’d suffered. He spoke instead of their supposed failures: their pauses, their questions, the moments they’d looked tired. He described each small human imperfection as if it were evidence in a trial.

“They listened,” he said. “Then they went home and couldn’t stop hearing me.”

“I’m sorry they suffered.”

“Do you believe I caused it?”

“I believe you want me to believe you did.”

His smile returned, but it no longer looked kind. “You’re careful.”

“I’m trying to be accurate.”

“Careful people always think accuracy will protect them.”

“I don’t think that.”

“Then what do you think?”

I glanced at the clock. Not because I was afraid of it, but because I’d promised the nurse I would check in halfway through. The nurse stood visible through the narrow pane in the door. When our eyes met, she gave the smallest nod.

“I think this conversation is affecting me,” I said. “And I think we should take a break.”

He laughed softly. “Already?”

“Yes.”

“You’ll come back?”

“I’ll consult with my supervisor before we decide what happens next.”

He rose. For a second, I wondered if he would say something designed to follow me into the hallway. Then he merely straightened his cuffs.

At the door, he turned. “You’ll think about what I said.”

“Probably,” I said. “And I’ll talk about it with someone.”

His expression closed.

The nurse walked him back to the ward. My supervisor joined me a minute later, as planned. I described the conversation without dressing it up as a contest I’d won.

Then I drank a glass of water.

The clock ticked on the shelf. I noticed it, and let myself look away.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Kidnapped whilst on holiday you find that a lifetime of pointless jobs has miraculously prepared you with all the necessary skills to save the day .
content:
### The Career Path

By the time I was thirty-four, I had held twenty-seven jobs and acquired no pension, no professional qualifications, and a deep suspicion of anyone who said, “It’ll only take a minute.”

I had sold novelty sunglasses from a kiosk. I had dressed as a snowman outside a garden centre in July. I had worked hotel reception, answered customer complaints for a broadband company, stacked tins in a supermarket, and spent one bewildering summer as the assistant to an escape-room game master.

None of this, I felt, had prepared me for a relaxing holiday on the island of Bellwether.

Then I was kidnapped.

It happened on my third afternoon, just as I was deciding whether a second ice cream counted as lunch. Two men in matching blue windbreakers approached me near the harbour.

“Are you Miss Vale?” one asked.

“That depends who’s asking.”

They looked at each other. “You’re coming with us.”

I considered shouting. Then the second man showed me a photograph of me leaving my hotel, which put a dampener on the whole idea.

They drove me to an abandoned aquarium on the far side of the island. The building smelled of salt, old carpet and the kind of damp that has given up hoping. In a dark room that had once housed tropical fish, I found three other hostages: Mr Bell, the island’s mayor; a tour guide named Pippa; and a twelve-year-old boy called Ollie, who was eating crisps with the calm of someone who had accepted that this was now his day.

The men in windbreakers were brothers. Their names were Dean and Colin. They had kidnapped the mayor to make him hand over the key to the town’s old lighthouse, which they planned to use as a hideout while they stole a collection of antique coins from the island museum.

“Why the lighthouse?” I asked.

“Because nobody goes there,” Dean said.

“People go there every day,” Pippa said. “It’s a tourist attraction.”

Dean frowned. “Not at night.”

The mayor folded his arms. “The lighthouse is being repaired. The light isn’t working.”

Outside, the sky had turned the colour of a bruised plum. The weather forecast had promised a storm, and the wind was already rattling the aquarium’s loose windows.

I was frightened. I was also, inconveniently, beginning to recognise the shape of the problem.

The brothers had a plan, but no system. They were arguing over who had the key, which one had the car, and whether the museum had “one of those silent alarms.” I had spent three years on a broadband complaints line listening to people explain why their router was personally insulting them. I knew how to keep a furious person talking.

“Dean,” I said, “you seem like the organised one.”

He stopped arguing with Colin.

“Me?”

“Clearly. Colin’s got the key.”

Colin checked his pocket. “I’ve got the car key.”

“Exactly,” I said. “Dean, you’re the one who knows what’s happening.”

Dean sat a little straighter. Colin looked annoyed. It was a small victory, but I had once worked a Christmas shift at a toy shop. I knew the value of keeping people occupied.

While the brothers began a low, serious disagreement about who was in charge, I looked around the room. On the far wall was an old staff door, half hidden behind a faded poster about penguins.

The door had a little window in it. Through the glass, I could see a corridor—and, beyond that, the aquarium’s public-address system.

I had worked an escape room for six months. The trick was not to look for a secret passage. The trick was to notice the thing everyone had decided was scenery.

Ollie followed my gaze. “You think we can get out?”

“I think,” I whispered, “that the people who designed this room wanted visitors to notice the penguins.”

Pippa moved closer. “And you want us to notice the door.”

“Exactly.”

The brothers were still arguing. I had also, thanks to my brief stint as a children’s entertainer, learned that a good distraction didn’t need to be clever. It only needed to be unexpected.

“Colin,” I called, “there’s a rat.”

He leapt onto a chair.

There was no rat.

But in the brief chaos that followed, the mayor shifted, Pippa reached the door, and Ollie—who had the quick fingers of someone raised on video games—found the old latch. The door opened.

We hurried into the corridor. I knew from my hotel-reception days that buildings often had a back route for staff. I also knew from supermarket shelf-stacking that when a storm rattles a building, you don’t put your weight on the wobbly things.

We found the staff exit, a store cupboard, and, most importantly, a wall phone with a handwritten label: **MANAGER’S OFFICE**.

The line was dead.

“Can you fix it?” Ollie asked.

“No,” I said. “But I can make it somebody else’s problem.”

I found the public-address microphone instead. My wedding-DJ career had lasted four weekends, but I had learned how to make my voice carry.

“Attention, Bellwether,” I announced. “This is an emergency. The mayor is at the old aquarium. The lighthouse is unlit. A storm is coming. Please send help.”

A crackle. Then silence.

I tried again.

This time, a voice answered through the speakers. “Who is this?”

“Someone who would like to leave the aquarium.”

The voice belonged to the harbourmaster. He had heard us. He was sending the coast guard and the police.

Then the lights went out.

A sound rolled across the island—a deep, mournful horn. The storm siren. Except it was coming from the lighthouse, and it wasn’t supposed to be working.

The mayor’s face changed. “The lighthouse keeper,” he said. “Old Mrs. Armitage. She must have gone up there to check the backup light.”

The brothers appeared at the end of the corridor, pale and furious. Behind them, rain lashed the windows.

For a second, nobody moved.

Then Colin said, “We can’t leave her up there.”

It was the first sensible thing either brother had said.

We all went together: the mayor, Pippa, Ollie, the two kidnappers, and me, who had once been paid to fold towels into swans. The lighthouse road was slick, but the harbourmaster met us halfway with a truck. At the top, we found Mrs. Armitage safe in the keeper’s room, trying to coax the backup lamp into life.

I had no idea how to fix a lighthouse. But I knew how to make a room full of panicked people useful.

“Pippa, keep Mrs. Armitage warm. Ollie, hold that torch steady. Mayor, tell us what needs doing. Dean and Colin—if you’re going to be helpful, now would be a marvellous time to start.”

They did.

By midnight, the lamp was shining over the water. The coast guard had rescued a fishing boat caught beyond the harbour, the museum’s coins were safely where they belonged, and Dean and Colin were sitting under police supervision, wrapped in emergency blankets.

The next morning, the mayor gave me a medal.

I thanked him, then asked if it came with a discount on ice cream.

It did.

I had the second one for lunch. For once, I didn’t feel guilty. After all, I had finally found a use for my résumé.

{prompt}
prompt: `` They said I pleaded guilty to murder . I prefer to look at it as taking pride in one 's work . ''
content:
### The Clean Job

“They said I pleaded guilty to murder. I prefer to look at it as taking pride in one’s work.”

The reporter stopped writing.

“That sounds like pride,” she said.

“It is.”

We were sitting in the prison’s visiting room, where everything was bolted down except the light. The light hummed overhead, indifferent to both of us.

She glanced at her notes. “You killed Arthur Bell.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

“Because I was paid.”

She waited for more. Reporters always do. They believe a reason ought to be larger than a fact.

I had been careful with Bell. Not kind—careful. There’s a difference. Kindness asks what a person needs. Care asks what the job requires. I knew his habits, his favorite restaurant, the hour he called his daughter on Sundays. I knew the names of his dogs. I knew he never wore his wedding ring because it pinched.

I knew all of that and still did what I was hired to do.

“Did you feel anything?” she asked.

“Not while I was working.”

“And afterward?”

“Afterward, I went home.”

She wrote that down. Perhaps she thought it made me monstrous. It was only true.

The door opened. A guard leaned in and said my visitor had arrived. The reporter looked up.

“Your daughter?”

“Yes.”

She gathered her papers. “Would you like me to stay?”

“No.”

She left, and a moment later my daughter came in.

Mara was thirty now. She had her mother’s dark eyes and my habit of looking at a room before entering it. She sat across from me, hands folded on the table.

“I read the article,” she said.

“I’m sorry.”

“Are you?”

It was a fair question. I had learned that most fair questions are the ones you can’t answer cleanly.

“I’m sorry you had to read it,” I said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“No.”

She looked down at her hands. “They say you were good at it.”

“I was.”

“That you were precise.”

“I was.”

“Do you want me to admire that?”

“No.”

“Then why say it?”

Because it was the one thing I had left to say about myself. Because skill sounds better than appetite. Because if I called it work, I could pretend I had been separate from the thing I did.

Instead, I said, “I don’t know.”

Mara’s mouth tightened. She had come expecting a confession, perhaps. A grand one. Something she could carry away and set beside the other things she knew about me: the father who taught her to ride a bicycle, the man who remembered birthdays, the man who had killed someone and gone home afterward.

“I used to think,” she said, “that if you were careful enough, you couldn’t be cruel.”

I watched her fingers press together.

“I was careful,” I said.

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No.”

The guard appeared at the door. Our time was up.

Mara stood. For a moment I thought she might reach across the table. She didn’t. She only looked at me as if she were trying to recognize someone she had once known.

Then she left.

The reporter returned after the door closed.

“Did she ask you to apologize?” she said.

“No.”

“What did she ask?”

I looked at the empty chair.

“Whether I wanted her to admire me.”

“And do you?”

For the first time that day, I had no answer ready.

Outside, a bell rang to mark the hour. I counted the notes without meaning to. The old habits remain, even when there is nothing left to measure.

“They said I pleaded guilty to murder,” I told her.

This time, I let the sentence stand on its own.

prompt: You live in a world without a regular day/night or season cycle . Every day is a different length , and nights have lasted what we know as years before . The world has always been like this . You are your peoples Time Keeper .
content:
**The Measure of Dark**

The first thing they taught me as a Time Keeper was never to promise a dawn.

“People will ask,” my mother said, placing the brass pendulum in my hands. “They’ll ask when the light is coming back. Tell them what you know. Not what they need to hear.”

I was seven measures old. A measure was the time it took our great clock to strike one thousand beats. It did not change when the sun vanished, or when the sky grew bright enough to turn the rooftops silver. Measures belonged to the clock. Days belonged to the sky.

And the sky had never kept a schedule.

Sometimes daylight lasted only a handful of measures. Sometimes it stretched so long that children were born, grew tall, and began families of their own before the sun slipped away. The darkness might last a night—or many years. No one knew why. No one remembered a world that had worked differently.

I became Keeper when my mother died, though I was still young enough to believe she might be waiting just beyond the next bell.

At the time, we had been in darkness for three thousand measures. Lamps burned in every window. The city’s gardens glowed with fungus, and farmers tended pale roots in warm tunnels beneath the earth. In the square, people gathered each day—not because the sun was expected, but because the clock struck there, and the sound reminded us that time was still passing.

For a while, that was enough.

Then the clock began to falter.

One beat went missing. Then another. A gear had cracked inside its iron housing, and the repair required a sliver of spring-steel thinner than a fingernail. We had no spare. The smiths searched their stores; the miners searched their carts. No one could find what we needed.

Without the clock, the measures would end. Work shifts would blur. Medicines would be given too soon or too late. People would lose the one thing the dark had not taken: their agreement about how long they had endured it.

So I sent word to every workshop in the city. I asked people to bring broken tools, buckles, toys, anything made of spring-steel. They came carrying the remains of their lives. A child brought the wind-up bird her grandfather had built. A baker brought the clasp from his wedding coat. A woman placed a tiny steel key in my palm and said it had opened her mother’s music box.

We melted them down together.

The smith drew out the metal. I held the lamp. The whole city crowded into the square while the clock lay open before us, its insides exposed like a sleeping heart. When the new spring was fitted, I raised my hand.

The clock ticked.

Once.

Twice.

Then it began again.

The crowd cheered. I wanted to cheer with them, but my mother’s words came back to me. A clock could tell us how long the dark had lasted. It could not tell us how long it would last.

Still, people began asking.

“Keeper,” they said, “will the light come soon?”

“I don’t know.”

“Before my baby can walk?”

“I don’t know.”

“Before the old ones are gone?”

I had no answer to give them that wouldn’t be a lie.

The dark went on. We marked births, deaths, repairs, harvests, and marriages. We marked the opening of a new tunnel and the collapse of an old one. The city changed around us, measure by measure. A girl who had once brought a wind-up bird to the clock square became a clockmaker herself. She was the one who finally taught me to mend the great clock without melting anyone’s memories.

Then, one day, during the quiet hour after the midday bell, a boy ran into the square.

“Keeper!” he shouted. “The eastern wall!”

People followed him up the stairs. I went last, carrying the record book.

At first, I saw nothing but the familiar dark: rooftops, lamps, the black sweep of the horizon. Then a thin gray line appeared beneath the clouds. It was so faint I thought it might be a trick of tired eyes.

The line widened.

Light spilled over the horizon—not warm, not golden, just light. It touched the tops of the walls and slid down the stones. People wept. Some laughed. A few fell to their knees. The boy clutched my sleeve and asked how long it would last.

I opened my record book.

The sun climbed. The city brightened. In the square, the great clock continued its steady ticking.

“How long?” the boy asked again.

I wrote down the measure and the moment the first ray struck the eastern wall.

“I don’t know,” I said.

He looked up at the growing sky. “But you’ll tell us when it goes?”

“Yes,” I said. “And when it comes back.”

For the first time, I understood what my mother had meant. A Time Keeper could not command the sky, or promise what it would do. We could only keep faith with what happened: the dark, the light, and all the life that passed between them.

So I rang the bell.

And the city stepped into day.
